#5465. Thinking About Taking Your House Off the Market? Read This First.

Between travel plans, family gatherings, and everything else this time of year can bring, selling your house may feel like just another squeeze on your calendar.

And if your house is already on the market, you may be wondering whether it’s worth keeping it listed. Maybe you’re even asking yourself: Wouldn’t it be easier to take a break and try again after the new year?

Before you decide, you should know there are some very real advantages that make staying on the market worthwhile.

Typically speaking, fewer people shop for homes toward the end of the year. And yes, that’s feeling even more true with rates where they are now. But here’s what you have to remember…

You don’t need dozens of people to fall in love with your house. You just need the right one. And the people who are still looking often have a pretty good reason they need to move.

Maybe they’ve accepted a new job that starts in early 2027.

Maybe their family needs more space and they’re trying to move during school breaks.

Or maybe something in their life has changed, and waiting until spring simply isn’t an option.

“Yes, things typically slow down in the weeks leading up to the holidays. But there are still people actively looking for homes and ready to pounce—or those who just entered the market on a short timeline and need to buy fast.”

The buyers looking now are exactly the types of buyers you want to see. They’re serious. They’re motivated. And they want to make this work.

Here’s another reason to think twice before taking your house off the market: other sellers may be having the exact same thought.

As the year winds down, fewer homeowners typically put their houses up for sale. And the latest data shows that’s happening again.

According to HousingWire Data, the number of new listings fell 13.4% from mid-October to mid-November 2026, and is down 7.1% year-over-year – the steepest annual decline since 2022. And that’s actually good for sellers who already have their homes listed for sale (see graph below):

For sellers who stay on the market, that means fewer of those fresh newly-listed houses to compete with. Sure, you may have other homeowners whose house has been listed for a while, but there won’t be nearly as many of those shiny, enticing “just listed” properties drawing your buyer’s attention away.

Keeping your house available gives it a chance to be seen while other homeowners are waiting for the calendar to turn. And that could mean more eyes on your house.

There’s also something to be said for keeping the momentum you’ve already built.

Your house is listed. The photos are done. Buyers can find it online. And your agent can continue marketing it to people who are actively looking.

If you take your house off the market, you could miss someone who’d be interested. But here’s the important part: staying on the market doesn’t mean you shouldn’t make adjustments.

If your house hasn’t attracted the offers you expected, this may be the perfect time to revisit your strategy.

Does the price still make sense compared to the competition?

Could better photos, staging, or a few small updates help your house stand out?

Would a price cut or upfront incentive be enough to get buyers interested?

Those are conversations worth having with your agent now, rather than assuming a new year will automatically bring a different result.

And you don’t have to put your life on hold for showings, either. Work with your agent to find a schedule that makes sense for you and your travel plans this season.

The end of the year may be busy for you, but that doesn't mean the housing market is closed for business. There are still motivated buyers looking and fewer new listings are coming onto the market.Before you decide to take your house off the market, talk to your agent about what’s happening locally and whether staying the course could help you get your house sold.

#5464. Oven Fires Surge This Time of Year—Here Is How Homeowners Can Protect Their Kitchen Over the Holidays

Let’s face it: The holiday season is when our ovens are working overtime.

Unfortunately, it’s also the prime time for an oven fire.

MoneyGeek recently analyzed seven years of fire department reports to the National Fire Incident Reporting System and compared each state's Thanksgiving Day cooking fires with its own average November day, from 2019 to 2025. Nationally, departments reported 3.72 times as many residential cooking fires on Thanksgiving.

And it's not just the turkey that could get ruined.

While a professional kitchen remodel averages $26,994, depending on the scope of the project and the location, according to Angi.com, fire damage might amp up that pricetag depending on whether cabinets, drywall, appliances, or partial finishes need to be removed and replaced.

Major structural damage can reach $100,000 if flames or water damaged wiring and plumbing or if the fire spread to adjacent rooms.

This is why experts recommend tried and true precautions homeowners can take to keep their home safe.

In the days leading up to the holidays, be sure to inspect the inside of your oven.

“Look specifically for older grease buildups,” says Steve Lockwood, owner of Mountain State Fire Protection, a fire safety equipment inspector and installer in Mesa, AZ.

“Over time, those can build up, become extremely hot, and they could ignite pretty easily.”

If you’re someone who routinely stores items in your oven, be sure to empty the space entirely—before you preheat it.

“Often people don’t realize they have plastic cutting boards and casserole dishes with plastic lids stored in their oven,” Sam Taylor, disaster public affairs program manager with the American Red Cross, tells Realtor.com.

“You don’t want to run the risk of melting those items in the oven.”

During the entire time you’re cooking a dish on your burners, stow all combustible materials away.

“Pay special attention to such items as plastic spatulas and utensils that can melt and catch fire, as well as wooden spoons, oven mitts, and paper products,” Taylor says.

Always make sure you’re not cooking foods on too-high temperatures, which can result in a fire; avoid dangerous bump-ins; and make sure pan handles don’t hang over the edge of the burners.

“This can cause the contents to spill and could cause burns or fire,” Lockwood says. And never wear a shirt with long, loose sleeves while you’re cooking.

“If you’re working over an open flame, that sleeve can catch fire,” says Taylor. “I always recommend wearing a different top that doesn’t have any fabric hanging near a flame.”

Whatever you do, never leave the house when your oven is on, Lockwood says.

“Where most people go wrong is walking away from the kitchen,” he says. Instead, keep an eye on your oven at all times. Tip: If you have a newer digital stove, pay special attention.

“A lot of these burners can be accidentally turned on just by leaning over them,” Lockwood says. “That’s why it’s a good practice to put the stove into a lockout mode to avoid an accidental turn on.”

Should a fire happen, keep the oven door closed, turn off the heat, reach for your kitchen extinguisher, and alert the authorities.

“Opening the oven door feeds the fire with oxygen,” Lockwood says. “In addition, while baking soda will work in a pinch, never use water on a grease fire.”

And, if a pot on your burner catches fire, turn off the heat and put a lid or baking sheet on it immediately to smother the fire, he adds.

#5463. Should You Wait for Lower Rates? Answers for Anyone Planning a 2027 Move.

When the family gathers around the table, the big housing headlines usually come up first. Are prices going to crash? What about a recession? (The data doesn’t point to either one.)

But by the time dessert comes out, the conversation tends to get more personal. That’s when people start talking about their own plans – whether to wait for lower rates and whether buying or selling actually makes sense right now.

Those are the questions that might shape your, your friends’, and family’s plans for 2027. So, let’s dig into each one.

Experts don’t see rates dropping much through 2027. Forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo all have rates landing between about 6.9% and 7.2% by the end of next year.

So, if you’re waiting for a big drop, you could be waiting a while.

And a smaller dip may not save as much as you’d think. On a $400,000 loan, going from 7.25% to 7% lowers the monthly principal and interest payment by only about $68 (see chart below):

Odds are, that’s not as much as you expected.

The bigger opportunity is the leverage buyers have right now. Realtor.com estimates the recent rise in rates cost a buyer with a $2,000 monthly budget more than $22,000 in purchasing power. But the typical price cut on a median-priced home is about $18,000, according to HousingWire Data.

In other words, a typical price cut today can win back most of the buying power higher rates took away. That’s why the deal you can negotiate now may matter more than waiting for rates to come down.

Another lingering question, what’s going to happen to home prices going forward? Every situation is different. But if you’re ready and the numbers work for you, forecasts show buying can pay off over time.

Based on the projections of over 100 experts and economists compiled by Fannie Mae, home prices will continue to rise nationally through at least 2031. That means a $400,000 home should gain over $58,000 in value over the next 5 years (see graph below):

That’s wealth you build just by owning your home, paying down your mortgage, and if prices rise in your area. That’s a far cry from experts saying there’s going to be a crash.

And since buyers today have more homes to choose from than they’ve had in recent years, you should be able to find a home that fits your budget so you can buy now and start building that long-term wealth through the years. But since price trends vary by local market, before you start looking, talk to an agent about what’s happening where you are.

While you may be hearing that more sellers are doing price cuts or making concessions, here’s some perspective you’ll want to consider. That doesn’t mean you have to make some big compromise to get your house sold or that it’s a bad time to sell.

If you price and prep your house right, you can likely still sell fast and for a good profit. Sure, your buyer may ask for a concession, but that’s all up for negotiation – and you likely have plenty of equity to sell and come out ahead.

And don’t forget it goes both ways. Most sellers are also buyers – odds are you are too. 78% of homebuyers are repeat buyers, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR) (see graph below). So, when you go to buy your next place, you can negotiate with that seller on terms, too.

Because if you have to be a little flexible on your sale, the sellers you buy your next house from will likely have to be flexible, too.

Right now, 43% of listings have a price cut, according to HousingWire Data. And Redfin reports nearly half of buyers are getting concessions from sellers, like help with closing costs. Those are things that will work to your benefit when it’s time to buy.

Rates aren’t expected to fall much, home prices are forecast to keep rising, and sellers usually get some flexibility back when they buy their next home. But whether to wait, buy, or sell is a big decision, and the right answer depends on your goals and your local market. If you’re weighing a move in 2027, connect with a local real estate agent to talk through your options so you can decide what’s right for you.

#5462. Mortgage Applications Rise to Their Highest Level in 5 Weeks Despite Rise in Rates

Mortgage applications increased last week, despite high interest rates, inflation concerns, and a wobbly stock market.

For the week ending Nov. 20, the Mortgage Bankers Association's Market Composite Index—a measure of total mortgage loan application volume—increased 6.1% on a seasonally adjusted basis from one week earlier.

The Purchase Index, which measures the volume of mortgage applications to purchase a single-family home, increased 5% from one week earlier after seasonal adjustment, though purchase applications are down 16% from a year ago.

The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed mortgages with conforming loan balances jumped to 7.38% this week, an increase from last week's rate of 7.31%, according to MBA calculations, and it's the highest level in five weeks.

A separate survey from Freddie Mac showed mortgage rates rose to 7.28%, up from  7.11% last week. A year ago at this time, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.26%.

"While mortgage rates increased slightly on a weekly average basis, rates declined over the course of the week, which likely spurred purchase application activity,” said Joel Kan, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist.

“Purchase applications reached their strongest weekly pace since September but remained well behind last year’s pace," he added.

Kan also noted that the share of borrowers relying on riskier adjustable-rate mortgage loans jumped to 11.5%—its highest level in more than a year.

"At 6.39%, the ARM mortgage rate was nearly a full percentage lower than the 30-year fixed rate last week," he said.

The share of FHA loan applications decreased to 15.9% from 16.1% the prior week. The VA share of total applications decreased to 12.4% from 12.8% the prior week. And the USDA share of total applications remained unchanged at 0.5%.

The refinance share of mortgage activity decreased to 40.1% from 41.1% the previous week, but was 51% lower than the same week one year ago, as homeowners remain locked in to their lower interest rates.

"Refinance activity was flat over the week with conventional applications showing a small increase while VA refinances dropped more than 11%," Kan said. The latest mortgage application data comes following a week of stock market volatility. On Friday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 briefly plunged into correction territory, defined as a 10% decline from their last peak.

The sell-off, driven by a wipeout in tech and AI stocks, came a day after Anthropic raised a staggering $81.34 billion during its IPO on Thursday, lifting the company's valuation to $1.414 trillion.Adding to the economic stress was an announcement on Wednesday from President Donald Trump that he's proposed new tariffs of up to 20% on China, the EU, and a dozen other major U.S. trading partners to take effect next year.

Mortgage rates are calculated based on several economic factors, while your loan term and credit score also influence the mortgage rate you qualify for. On the economic side, rates tend to track the 10-year Treasury note, since most 30-year mortgages are paid off or refinanced in roughly eight to 11 years.

That makes the duration on the loans roughly comparable, and mortgage lenders use the 10-year Treasury as a benchmark for setting rates, adding on a risk premium.

Long-term yields for Treasury notes are determined by a number of factors, including the supply of and demand for U.S. government debt, and investor expectations for inflation over the life of the bonds.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5461. FHFA Increases Conforming Loan Limit by $22k for 2027

The Federal Housing and Finance Authority (FHFA) has announced a new conforming loan limit (the maximum dollar amount for a conventional mortgage) for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac mortgages in 2027. The new limit for one-unit properties will be $855,400, up $22,650 from 2026’s limit.

The Housing and Economic Recovery Act (HERA) requires FHFA to adjust the Enterprises’ baseline conforming loan limit each year to reflect the change in the average U.S. home price, according to a release. As the organization’s research found that home prices were up 2.72% on average from Q3 2025 to Q3 2026, the FHFA said that the conforming loan limit has increased on the same baseline.

In addition, high cost areas (where 115% of the local median home value exceeds the baseline conforming loan limit) have a higher limit due to HERA, according to a release. The high cost area limit sits at a ceiling of 150% the baseline limit, which in 2027 will be $1,283,100.

The FHFA also noted special statutory provisions establishing different loan limits for Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands. In these areas, the baseline loan limit and the ceiling loan limit for one-unit properties will be $1,283,100 and $1,924,650, respectively.

Due to rising home values, the FHFA stated that the conforming loan limit will be higher in all but 24 U.S. counties or county equivalents.

#5460. Dell and HP beat expectations, but their fortunes are diverging as AI dynamics crush the PC market

Dell Technologies Inc. and HP Inc. delivered strong earnings and revenue beats as they posted their latest financial results today.

However, the companies have very different prospects going forward as they try to come to terms with the diverging fortunes of the artificial intelligence server and personal computer markets they serve.

Dell reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $9.45 per share on revenue of $54.94 billion, a stunning result that blew past Wall Street’s expectations of just $6.59 per share in earnings and $49.32 billion in sales.

The company’s revenue more than doubled from a year earlier thanks to the sky-high demand for the AI servers and related data center infrastructure equipment it sells. Dell’s Infrastructure Solutions Group delivered sales of $41.97 billion during the quarter, far in excess of the Street’s target of $35.27 billion. Of that, around $22 billion came from direct AI-optimized server sales, the company said. That segment was up 291% annually.

“We are now a different company, with the Infrastructure Solutions Group driving the vast majority of our profit and growth,” said Dell Vice Chairman and Chief Operating Officer Jeff Clarke (pictured). He added that Dell now has more than 7,500 customers buying its AI servers.

The Street liked what it saw, with Dell’s stock rising more than 3% after hours, putting the brakes on an 11% decline earlier, during the regular trading session. Update: However, on another down day for tech stocks Wednesday, Dell’s shares were falling almost 8% before the market cut some of those losses and Dell was falling only a fraction of a point.

Dell’s performance in the quarter sets a new precedent for infrastructure systems companies, said longtime technology industry analyst Dave Vellante, chief analyst at theCUBE Research, SiliconANGLE Media’s sister market research firm.

“Dell has transformed from a PC company into a dominant enterprise infrastructure provider and industry bellwether,” he said. “What’s most astounding to me is that I’ve always considered AWS to be Dell’s most formidable competitor. Dell is now significantly larger than AWS on a trailing 12-month revenue basis and is growing at a rate that’s more than double that of AWS, Azure and on a par with Google Cloud.”

Clarke told analysts on a conference call that the company has a significant competitive advantage over its rivals on the software side, which enables customers to get their servers up and running in data centers within hours of taking delivery of them. “That allows customers to convert backlog into revenue sooner and more reliably,” he added.

Dell is raising its forecast for AI servers in the coming fiscal years, and now sees sales rising to a staggering $78 billion, ahead of the Street’s target of $74 billion. At present, the company has an even bigger order backlog of $132.3 billion for AI servers. “Every order is verified for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power,” Clarke told analysts in response to a question about the reliability of that backlog.

Vellante said Dell’s operating leverage is just as impressive, with its operating income, net profit and earnings per share all growing at rates over two-times its revenue growth.

“Its massive backlog and strong product execution allow it to be selective,” the analyst said. “Thus the quality of its revenue and its backlog is very high, and the company is well-positioned for the next several quarters. Current market signals point to a structural change in tech where vendors that are in a position to help customers transform and drive new levels of productivity are poised to win over the long term. We increasingly see Dell as one of those leaders.”

Besides servers, Dell still has a big business in the PC market. Its Client Services Group was once the company’s biggest segment, but its revenue is now dwarfed by AI server sales. During the quarter, it generated revenue of $12.89 billion, below the Street’s forecast of $14.33 billion.

The reason for that miss is that the global PC market is currently enduring a sharp decline. Last month, Gartner Inc. reported a stunning 22% drop in global PC shipments in the third quarter, citing the increased costs of components such as memory chips, which have led to higher prices and compelled many people to hold onto their older laptops for longer.

The miserable state of PC sales makes HP’s latest quarterly results seem even more impressive than they were. However, the company’s cautious outlook suggests that its incoming Chief Executive Emma Walmsley (pictured, right) will have her work cut out when she assumes the role full time on Jan. 4, when she’s slated to take over from interim CEO Bruce Broussard.

HP reported fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of 83 cents per share, surpassing the analyst consensus estimate that called for a profit of just 75 cents per share. Revenue for the period came to $16 billion, up 9% and above the Street’s target of $15.4 billion.

HP’s stock briefly surged more than 17% after-hours, before promptly surrendering all of those gains in under an hour. It was down just under a percentage point at the time of writing. Update: On Wednesday, investors appeared to change their minds again, as the stock was rising more than 12%.

Investors had low expectations of HP given the shoddy state of the PC market. The company has been trying to mitigate the situation somewhat by raising its prices, but it couldn’t stop its profit margins from declining in the quarter.

The market was eagerly anticipating HP’s guidance to try and get a lid on whether or not the PC market has any prospect of recovery in the near future, but the company disappointed by refusing to provide any. All it would say is that it forecasts free cash flow in the current quarter to be $3 billion, plus or minus $100 million. Analysts are targeting free cash flow of $3.3 billion.

HP hasn’t been helped by the fact that it has been without a CEO since PayPal Holdings Inc. surprisingly swooped in to poach its former leader Enrique Lores in February. Broussard has held the fort for close to nine months now, but the company did at least finally name a successor in Walmsley, who will begin her tenure next year. She formerly led the pharmaceutical giant GSK Plc.

Walmsley has a tough act to follow, however, for Broussard has done rather well in his efforts to cope with the PC market downturn and the higher component costs. Although the stock was up and down today, it’s still up 25% in the year to date.

#5458. What Next-Gen Real Estate Leaders Are Leaving Behind and Embracing Instead

Above, from left, Eric Fite, Jack Markham, Marisela Harper, Lori Muller and Adrian Provost

“All the technology in the world doesn’t matter unless it makes a fundamental impact on the relationship with the client, the way we serve them. That’s our true north.”

That was the sentiment summed up by Eric Fite, COO of CENTURY 21 Judge Fite Company in Dallas/Fort Worth, when moderating a recent panel of up-and-coming brokerage leaders about what old ways they are leaving behind and what innovative new approaches they are bringing to the fore.

AI and technology and how they can best be used dominated the discussion, but panelists also shared some of the ways they are reimagining traditional business practices to support their agents in the session titled, “Next-Gen Leaders and Their Powerful New Approach to Business,” held this past October at RISMedia’s CEO Exchange in Washington, D.C.

In addition to Fite, the panel included Marisela Harper, broker/owner of ClearView Realty; Adrian Provost, CEO of ONE Terminus & LEVEL; Lori Muller, president of Fathom Realty; and Jack Markham, chief marketing officer at Inside Real Estate.

The group also shared insights into how they are positioning their tech stacks and CRMs, how they are viewing their data and data ownership and control,as well as the future of AI and how it can assist agents through automation.

“I think everybody’s realizing that the CRM is not necessarily your tech stack,” said Markham when asked what old beliefs most forward-thinking brokerages have already abandoned. “Traditionally, you would pick a CRM, and that’s where your data is; that’s who owns the workflows. But quite honestly, the smartest brokers are realizing that the tech stack is way more than your CRM.

“Most teams are running two to three CRMs. And that’s not because everybody loves using multiple CRMs. They do it because it’s a fear of loss. They do it because if I drop a tech stack, if I drop a tool, I don’t want to lose my data. And so they’re doing it as insurance. So I think most of the smart brokers today are realizing they don’t need more tools in the tech stack. They don’t need another tool, another app. What they need is something to absorb the tech stack, something that’s going to empower their data so their agents think less about where they log in and more about how to drive conversations.”

Provost said he views the “tech stack,” or the set of software tools, apps and technologies a company uses, as more of a folder, and a platform as more of an operating system.

“Ultimately, what I look for is how (tech) helps close certain loops that lead to that appointment-to-close loop, and then to that close-to-repeat-and-referral-business. I think that if it’s something that isn’t touching one of those or enhancing the agent’s ability to perform, then it probably doesn’t really belong in the tech or in the platform.”

Fite then turned the conversation to AI, asking panelists how they are using it and consumer behavior data to identify when and how an agent should engage a consumer.

“With consumer behavior data, that data is your opportunity,” Muller said. “It’s your opportunity to be strategic with what you’re going to do with it, how you’re going to utilize it. And then AI is the actual action step. It’s how you take action with that data to create a result.”

Markham said it’s all about control over data.

“The uncomfortable question for most brokers is, if you decided to leave your tools or your tech stack, could you take your data with you? And the answer most likely for most brokers in the industry is no,” he said. “They find out far too late that they can’t take it with them. Real ownership of data means you control that data no matter what CRM or tech tool you’re using.”

On a question about what work AI should be doing for a human, Provost said:

“I look at it from an operational standpoint. How can AI assist me and my agents in enhancing our service to our clients? And in my case, my clients being the agent. And so I think that humans need to always be in the loop. There should never be one point where they’re disconnected, but it should be streamlined, and we should be able to have AI connect components that don’t normally talk to one another so we can perform better and elevate that entire experience for whoever’s on the opposite end of it.”

Muller added that AI can help with automating transaction management, marketing solutions, social media, communication or “B- and C-level” operational tasks, while leaving more time for the most important aspect of the business—client relationships.

“No matter who tries to destroy the real estate industry, you can’t take the relational side away from the Realtor® and the consumer. AI is not going to do it. Technology’s not going to do it. That’s the most important thing we have to look at,” she said.

How does the next generation of real estate business leaders view traditional ways of supporting agents, or “loving on them,” as the panel discussed?

“We really do everything so strategically to love on the agent, down to when we built our office four years ago,” said Harper. “We built this big hub and we put our offices right where people that come in can see us. And that’s done on purpose. We have our staff completely trained to love on the agent. We also train our mentors to love on the agents. And when I say love, that’s really being intentionally present with them, spending the time to go to their weddings, go to the baby showers, attend the funerals because that’s a time when they really need just someone to be there for them.”

She added, “And one of the most important things on that contact card is the agent’s birthday. And that might seem so silly, but when I open my calendar for the day, I see whose birthday it is and that’s the first phone call I make just to call them and wish them a happy birthday. Of course, we do the birthday cards and the gift card and all of that, but the call just to wish them happy birthday, see how they’re doing, it goes over so well. They absolutely love it.”

Here are some more notable quotes from the session:

What’s most important when an agent leaves the brokerage?

Lori Muller: When an agent leaves, sometimes they leave because they think the grass is greener on the other side, and they get over there and it’s not. So I think it’s super important to have some type of exit strategy when an agent leaves and have a conversation to say, “Hey, what could we have done better? What was the situation that caused you to leave?” And it’s a teaching moment for both people. We also just recently did a comeback campaign where we called agents that have left over the last two years, and we have had almost a 25% return rate.

Are we heading toward a world where technology becomes table stakes and culture, service and execution become the real differentiators?

Jack Markham: I think you could take two people and give them the same tech stack, and what’s really going to separate them is not necessarily the tools that you’re using. It’s once you plug in your data, right? Once you plug in those relationships, once you plug in the trust, once you plug in the consumer behaviors that you’ve been tracking and the history behind that, it becomes your thumbprint. What’s unique and can’t be copied is all the history there. It’s all the relationships, it’s all the trust that becomes your thumbprint. And so that can never really be duplicated.

What’s the one move you would make over the next 12 months to better position your brokerage and your agents for where the industry is going?

Jack Markham: Figure out if you own your data. Meaning if you left today, some of your tools, could you take them with you? And if the answer is no, then I would fix that.

Marisela Harper: I would say just be super, super present because (agents) need that from you, and just show the love. And when I say show the love, I really mean truly say, “I love you.” Sometimes people might know that you love them, but they need to hear it too.

Lori Muller: Embrace your relationship with not only your technology, but your people. Longevity is in the relationship with the people; tech stack and your technology is constantly changing.

Adrian Provost: Move away from tech stacks completely and create platforms. The old days are completely over. Whatever you need, you can literally build it. And so I would move away from being so reliant on a tech stack and subscriptions and actually figure out what it is that your agents need and provide that to them.

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.

#5457. New-Home Sales Surge as Builders Slash Prices to Move Inventory

New -home sales surged in October as prices dropped, according to the latest data from the U.S. Census Bureau.

Sales of new single-family homes hit 701,000 in October, 14.2% above what they were in September and 7.5% above October 2025. Meanwhile, the median sales price hit $391,300, 0.3% below September 2026 and 3.2% below October 2025.

That was driven entirely by a surge in the South, which saw a 36.2% increase from last month and a 24.7% increase from October 2025. Northeast sales plummeted 40.0% month over month and 63.4% year over year, and the Midwest and West also saw declines.

This comes after new-home sales fell 0.6% month over month, 5.3% year over year in September, to 676,000. New-home sales were running 2.9% below 2025 numbers, Realtor.com® economists found. The median sales price in September for new homes fell 3.9% year over year to $400,400.

Realtor.com Senior Economist Joel Berner noted that new home sales are still 3% below where they were in the first 10 months of 2025. And housing inventory remains low.

"Builders are lowering prices to meet demand, and the median new home sales price remains well below the median existing home sales price," Berner said.

The National Association of Home Builders found that new homes are nearly $40,000 less expensive than existing homes. Single-family housing starts rose 4% last month amid an uneven year. The latest Realtor.com quarterly construction insights report shows that prices on new homes are holding steady, but builders are having to get creative to attract buyers.

Meanwhile, major homebuilders have reported large year-over-year declines in revenue. This week, the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index plunged to a 14-year low.

The tough environment has forced builders to get creative.

"Builders are exercising caution, preferring to line up a buyer for their homes before starting work on them rather than building as many spec homes," Berner said. "New construction remains a strong alternative to the existing home segment, offering savings on mortgage rates, sale prices, and total cost of ownership."

Simon Boag, CEO of Aro Homes, says his company opted for across-the-board price cuts on its prefabricated homes, slashing about $12 million off the asking price of its overall housing stock. It ended up holding an auction to sell a batch of 10 homes, which seems to have worked. About eight of the homes found buyers.

Boag tells Realtor.com that he looks at past recessions when many buyers remained in the market, even if they weren't looking aggressively. Homebuilders have to accept lower margins, but there are buyers looking for homes.

"You look at a decent homebuilder margin in the 20% range, but at 17%, you're still a viable entity," Boag says. "The business model is about, 'OK markets move all the time,' and how do you deal with that."

For buyers, the market may have a higher barrier to entry in the high interest rate environment. That means preparation is essential.

Earlier this week, the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index showed home values fell for the 16th straight month.

Jeffrey Ruben, president of home lending at WSFS Bank, expects the "tug of war" between high mortgage rates and affordability constraints limiting buyers in 2027.

"While this is a good sign for home builders, it doesn't indicate what the market shows as a whole," Ruben said. "We are seeing the data signal movement toward a buyer's market. This is seen more clearly through existing home sales with time on market, overall sales, and total inventory."

He said buyers should be looking beyond standard resale listings and comparing the total monthly payment structure across both new and existing homes.

"Connecting with a lender early to evaluate builder incentives alongside traditional financing options can help buyers identify opportunities in the current market without stretching their household budget," he said.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

A nor'easter and even a "bomb cyclone" are predicted to slam the Northeast on Thanksgiving this year, putting millions in a path of destruction not seen on the holiday for decades.

Heavy rain, high winds, and coastal impacts to the East Coast are said to begin on Wednesday and carry through Thanksgiving, according to NOAA's Weather Prediction Center.

The biggest impact will be seen starting in the Southeast, before moving its way to the Northeast, Great Lakes, and Ohio Valley.

While flooding is a major consideration, meteorologists are more concerned about the powerful winds accompanying the storm, which could result in tree damage, power outages, and other disasters for homeowners to contend with on the big day.

The storm will ramp up in the Southeast on Wednesday, according to The Weather Channel, with rain, wind, and coastal flooding causing hazardous conditions for travelers heading home for the holiday.

Because temperatures have dropped as well, snow is also likely in parts of Missouri and Illinois beginning later in the day, continuing into the night, into Thanksgiving.

By Thanksgiving Thursday, the storm will have made its way north into the mid-Atlantic and Ohio Valley, before steadily moving into New England by afternoon or evening.

While wind is top of mind given the milestone parade, significant coastal flooding along the East Coast is poised to cause beach erosion, flooded coastal streets, and potential structural damage.

Moderate to major flooding is possible from Georgia to Long Island, alongside at least minor flooding in New England, with any heavy rain during high tide worsening the inundation, says Weather.com.

Peak water levels will hit Georgia and South Carolina on Wednesday morning, before shifting north to North Carolina, Virginia, Delaware, the Jersey Shore, and Long Island on Thanksgiving morning, and reaching coastal New England by Thursday and Friday midday.

Conditions could be especially severe in the mid-Atlantic, with widespread road flooding expected across Jersey Shore communities such as Atlantic City and Ocean City, water levels in Cape May and coastal Delaware potentially hitting their highest mark since January 2016, and Ocean City, MD, approaching its 1998 all-time record.

A high wind watch is in effect for all of Thanksgiving Day in New York City, according to local reports, with wind gusts of up to 60 mph possible.

The parade is scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. EST on Thursday, on Manhattan’s Upper West Side.

"There is a significant risk that gusty winds ahead of the nor’easter cause the parade balloons to at least be lower than usual, and it’s possible they are not able to fly at all," AccuWeather Vice President of Forecast Operations Dan DePodwin said.

"This scenario is most likely should the storm move a bit more quickly up the coast. If it’s slower, the wind may intensify after the parade is over."

The current wind forecasts for New York City are higher than the wind thresholds for the Thanksgiving Day Parade balloons.

Sustained winds must remain below 23 mph and gusts have to be lower than 34 mph for the balloons to fly.

The last balloon grounding was in 1971, but the parade has never been canceled due to weather in its 100-year history.

It remains to be seen if the parade will carry out as planned, but New York City Emergency Management Commissioner Christina Farrell told local outlet WABC that one last-minute move the city is considering would be to start the parade earlier than 8:30 a.m., beating the bad weather to the punch.

Power outages and tree damage are possible, according to the Weather Prediction Center, as wind gusts of 50-plus mph are forecasted along the coast with 40-plus mph gusts inland into the Interstate-95 corridor through at least Friday.

As of Monday evening, the National Weather Service warned that “tree damage and power outages will be possible” from the storm on Thanksgiving Day.

The forecasts put the strongest gusts along the mid-Atlantic coast and inland corridors on Thursday. Along the New Jersey shore and Delaware beaches, gusts will reach 50 to 60 mph—with 40 to 50 mph inland—prompting NWS Mount Holly to issue a high wind watch for the coastal strip from late Wednesday night through late Thursday night.

Farther south, Southeast Virginia and Northeast North Carolina face 2 to 3 inches of rain alongside east to northeast gusts of 40 to 50 mph inland and potentially 50 to 60 mph on the coast, where NWS Wakefield noted a high wind watch may be needed. Meanwhile, Washington, DC, Baltimore, and Northern Virginia can expect 1 to 3 inches of rain and Thanksgiving Day gusts of 35 to 50 mph, which NWS Sterling warned could be “strong to perhaps damaging.”

The threat shifts northward later in the day, with Southern New England forecast to see gusts of 40 to 55 mph and up to 60 mph on Cape Cod and the islands. According to NWS Boston, the strongest winds in that region will arrive on Thursday night. In Rhode Island, forecasters specifically note the potential for isolated power outages late Thursday night and overnight, with coastal areas facing the highest risk.

Meanwhile, California has its own winter weather whirlwind to contend with, including massive waves battering the coastline.

According to the NWS, record-breaking king tides, combined with elevated surf and a large Pacific swell, are expected to bring significant coastal flooding to Southern California during this Thanksgiving week, with the greatest impacts anticipated Wednesday and Thursday, potentially flooding coastal properties and causing significant beach erosion.

“A series of winter storms is impacting California, bringing heavy rain, mountain snow, and potentially hazardous travel conditions,” the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services said on Friday.

The mayor of San Francisco warned of “high tides and rain that this city has never seen before,” in the days leading up to the holiday, asking the public to avoid all but essential travel. The National Weather Service in the Bay Area added low areas would be prone to flooding, including San Francisco International Airport, which would be an added hindrance to travel to say the least.

Meanwhile, Southern California cities such as Newport Beach, Seal Beach, and Long Beach have put up miles of sand berms, some 15 feet tall or higher, to try to keep the ocean back, according to The Washington Post.

This weather seems to be a perfect storm of the warm waters of record-breaking El Niño colliding with an extra-high “king tide,” which the area already had to contend with a few weeks ago.

"In California, tides will be about half a foot higher than the highest in October," physical oceanographer Greg Dusek told Weather.com.

"This means that even if El Niño doesn't increase water levels further, there will be significant flooding along the California coast," Dusek said.

Forecasts predict the worst of the storms could strike on Tuesday and Wednesday night into Thanksgiving Day.

All season long, the "Dancing with the Stars" judges recognized Amber Glenn's competitive nature, but now that the season has come to an end, the Olympic figure skater is proving that she has been a team player all along.

Glen came in second place in the competition dance series, with two-time Paralympian Ezra Frech taking home the coveted Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy.

And while the contestants share a spot on Team USA—for which they've both brought home gold medals—they quickly bonded in the competition as their professional dance partners, Pasha Pashkov and Daniella Karagach, are married.

When asked how she felt about the results after the finale, Glenn told Extra she "couldn't ask for a better result," and described a "triumphant feeling" as she walked away from Season 35 having earned 10s across the board in all three of her final performances.

"From day one, we all met up, had a little dinner over at their house, and we said, 'We wanna go 1-2,'" she explained to the outlet. "And we didn't specify, like, whatever happens, happens, but the fact that we came in here and we both got those perfect scores. We both did everything we could and it was truly in the hands of the people at home. I'm really proud of what we did and I'm really, really happy that Team USA took it home."

The group—who have been unofficially dubbed "Team USA and the Pashkovs" by fans and even the official U.S. Olympic and Paralmypic team all season—have been close collaborators throughout the competition.

During the Nov. 10 episode, when teams were paired off and required to compete in two-on-two dance-offs, Glenn and Pashkov and Frech and Karagach put a friendly spin on the format by switching partners mid-choreography as they performed a Rumba to "The Boy Is Mine" by Brandy and Monica.

"It felt more like a team dance than anything else," Karagach told Us magazine. "We came together ,and we had the best time sharing the dance floor, and we couldn't also not end swapping partners because I've always wanted to dance with Amber, and Ezra and Pasha secretly wanted to dance with each other. So that was fun."

The competitors-turned-pals took to social media to share plenty of heartwarming behind-the-scenes moments throughout the experience, providing a glimpse at what their down time is like between rehearsals. In one Sept. 18 post, Pashkov wrote, "We're a tightly-knit fam now."

In a post-finale interview with Deadline, Glenn described the moment she had realized Frech would win. The Plano, TX native said, "I don't know if I felt as many emotions watching a performance as I did when watching Ezra and Dani. It was like, at first, it's excitement. I'm like, 'I love that Linkin Park [song].' And then horror, fear, and like, panic.'"

The moment Glenn was referring to was the malfunction in which Frech's prosthetic fell off mid-performance. Frech and Karagach quickly communicated while dancing, allowing him to secure it into place properly and complete the routine.

"I think I gasped so loud I threw my rib out again," Glenn continued. "So then, the physical pain and just like, fear, panic, and then just awe, inspiration, something you feel in your core. I know that's a saying, but like you feel it in your gut, and it takes your breath away, and that's what it was."

Glenn said that in that moment, she "was like, 'They won.'" She even added that she "would feel bad" if she had taken home the trophy after seeing Frech and Karagach pull off "such a perfect dance" after "working so hard for it all season."

#5450. Marlowe raises $277M to build inference clusters with chips from Nvidia rivals

Artificial intelligence infrastructure startup Marlowe AI Inc. has closed a huge $227 million seed round led by Accel.

Bessemer, Altimeter, Emergence Capital and a number of other institutional bakers chipped in as well. They were joined by a large group of angel investors that included the chief executives of Palo Alto Networks Inc, Uber Technologies Inc., Box Inc. and Dropbox Inc. GeekWire reported on Monday that Marlowe is valued at $1.15 billion.

Marlowe was founded last year by CEO Dan Lewis and Chief Technology Officer Kutta Srinivasan. Lewis previously headed the Microsoft Corp. unit responsible for Copilot Studio, the tech giant’s AI agent development tool. Srinivasan was the techical lead of the company’s AI infrastructure group.

Marlowe is building AI data centers for inference workloads. The company will optimize each facility for a specific inference workload category by tailoring its chip mix, network configuration and software. Marlowe believes that its approach will provide better hardware efficiency than general-purpose graphics card clusters.

“Even modest gains in network architecture, power oversubscription, AI-driven fleet operations, and workload-specific inference optimization multiply to create a durable, 2-3x overall advantage in performance, availability, resiliency, and cost,” Lewis and Srinivasan wrote in Marlowe’s launch blog post.

The company plans to bring its first data center online  next month. It’s based on hardware from Etched Inc., an inference chip startup that was valued at $21 billion in August.

Graphics cards often use only a small fraction of their maximum clock speed to avoid overheating. Etched’s chip is less prone to overheating and can therefore operate at higher clock speeds, which boosts model performance. The company says that its accelerator provides “multiple times the FLOPs density” of graphics cards.

Etched ships its chips as part of custom-made inference racks. According to the company, the systems feature an interconnect that can perform some data movement tasks more than four times faster than competing silicon. Etched’s rack design also includes custom power management and cooling components.

Marlowe’s second facility will come online in the second quarter of 2027. It will host racks based on Advanced Micro Devices Inc.’s Helios design. A Helios rack hosts 72 AMD graphics cards along with central processing units and Pensando data processing units, or DPUs. The DPUs offload networking tasks from the other chips to leave more computing capacity for AI models.

Helios racks’ networking and power delivery links are arranged in a configuration that reduces the need for manual cable maintenance. Additionally, the coolant lines feature a so-called quick-disconnect design. They can be plugged and unplugged without the specialized tools usually needed for the task.

GeekWire reported that Marlowe has also signed a letter of intent for a third data center. According to the publication, each of the company’s planned facilities will provide tens of megawatts of computing capacity. One megawatt is enough to power several hundred homes.

Marlowe will use the proceeds from its seed round to finance hardware purchases and hire engineers.

#5448. The Home Audit That Could Save Homeowners Thousands—and Cost You Only $50

With housing costs skyrocketing, every little bit helps—and sometimes, there are options even longtime homeowners are unaware of.

For example, a homeowner recently turned to Reddit to vent about humidity and outdoor air entering their home. They received quotes for an energy audit ranging from $100 to $200 and asked if this service is actually worth it.

Someone from Connecticut replied saying they paid only $50 for the same type of audit, thanks to a subsidy from their electric company—and depending on your location, utility provider, and/or income, you could also qualify for a subsidized or even free energy audit.

While experts agree that a $50 assessment is less common, even paying a few hundred for one may save you thousands of dollars down the road. That's because it can uncover hidden air leaks that may contribute to higher utility bills and damaging moisture issues.

“When you seal air leaks, you may prevent water vapor inside your house from turning into liquid inside your walls. This eliminates the need for costly wood rot and mold issues that may lead to $5,000 or more in repairs and reduces wear and tear on your HVAC unit,” explains Andrew Pho, a home renovation and improvement expert at Mister Balustealing in Toronto.

Energy audits are designed to find what’s causing energy loss in your home, but they’re not all created equal.

Before booking one, confirm what it includes.

“At the very least, it should consist of a blower-door test (a blower fan is set up in a doorway to measure how much air is leaking in or out of the home), check the levels of insulation in your attic, walls, etc., and look at your HVAC system to make sure it’s running efficiently,” says Dennis Vong, founder and owner of Inland Power Wash in Orange County, CA.

Clear, written suggestions on how to improve the energy efficiency of your home are important as well.

“Additionally, you may want to ask if minor fixes like caulking and weatherstripping are included in the audit or available for an additional cost,” Vong explains.

Niki O'Brien, operations manager at Custom Exteriors in Loveland, CO, reinforces the importance of ensuring your home has proper insulation and ventilation in your attic.

“It can prevent dangerous freeze/thaw cycles that can trap moisture and lead to ice damming and interior leaks,” O’Brien says.

If your goal is to improve energy efficiency and reduce the risk of needing repairs, an energy audit is a good idea.

According to Energy Star, proper insulation and air sealing can cut your heating and cooling bills by as much as 15% on average.

“If you spend $200 a month on heating and cooling, that could mean savings of about $30 a month, or $360 a year,” Vong explains.

O’Brien has experienced the benefits of an energy audit firsthand.

“We have seen many cases, including a home we owned personally, that needed additional insulation and resulted in lower energy costs,” says O’Brien.

At the end of the day, the information you get from an energy audit will absolutely save you money in the long run.

“Whether that means getting new, energy-efficient products, adding additional weather proofing to existing systems, or repairing/replacing caulking, insulation, or creating effective ventilation, eventually it will surpass the cost of an audit,” O’Brien adds.

According to the Department of Energy, an energy audit will typically run you between $250 and $600. The good news is you may be able to get one at a subsidized rate.

“I recommend calling your gas and electric providers to see if they offer energy audits at a subsidized rate and what rebates may be available if you were to make any energy improvements to your home,” says Vong.

Aaron Christy, founder and owner of Indy Roof & Restoration in Indianapolis, says that in Indianapolis, for example, AES Indiana offers all of its customers a no-cost virtual assessment, and a free in-home assessment if you meet certain income limits.

Your state may also offer a no-cost assessment.

“In my state, Massachusetts, there’s the Mass Save Program, which provides free audits to qualifying homeowners, renters, and landlords,” explains Ted Dow, vice president of delivery at Power Home Remodeling in Boston.

While you’re waiting for an audit, you can perform your own DIY assessment.

Make sure the weatherstripping around your doors and windows isn’t falling apart, check for any dripping faucets or leaking pipes, and make sure your gutters are draining properly away from your foundation.

“Just remember that it’s best to leave the more specialized services to the pros,” adds Vong.

#5447. Attached Homes Drive Salt Lake City’s New-Home Sales Growth

New home demand in Salt Lake City is increasingly splitting along product lines, with attached housing gaining momentum while detached sales remain comparatively flat.

In September, annualized new-home sales across the metro topped 2,800 units, up roughly 4% from a year ago. Attached housing drove much of the gain, with annualized sales reaching 1,350 units, a 10% increase year over year. Meanwhile, detached sales remained slightly higher at 1,450 units but edged down 0.7% from last year.

Although detached homes still accounted for more sales in absolute terms, virtually all of the market’s recent growth stemmed from attached product. Active project counts showed a similar pattern. As of November, Salt Lake City had 92 active detached new-home projects, down 3.2%, compared with 65 attached projects, up 3.2%.

Pricing helps explain why attached housing may be resonating with buyers, especially given today’s affordability challenges. As of July, the average list price for a new detached home was roughly $738,000, up 11% from a year earlier, while new attached homes averaged approximately $470,000, up about 4%. That puts the difference between the two averages at more than $268,000, although it is important to note that attached and detached homes differ in size, location, design, and community mix.

The distribution of closings reinforces that distinction. In the past 12 months ending August, attached new-home closings were concentrated heavily in lower price bands, particularly between $350,000 and $450,000. Detached closings were distributed much more broadly, with the most substantial shares falling between $450,000 and $650,000.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

#5445. New-Home Sales See Welcome Shift, but Not an Overall Improvement

With housing construction continuing to face supply chain and affordability challenges, the latest data from the U.S. Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development saw new-home sales experience a welcome shift upward.

New-home sales jumped 14.2% in October to a rate of 701,000, up from a revised rate of 614,000 in September (originally 676,000). This was also up 7.5% year-over-year.

While a positive shift for the construction industry, the shift is notably due entirely to growth in the South. While all three other regions were down both month-over-month and year-over-year to varying degrees, the South was up 36.2% month-over-month and 24.7% year-over-year.

Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington, National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) assistant vice president for forecasting and analysis, noted that while any increase in new-home sales is “encouraging,” it is “too early to interpret the gain as a sustained recovery in housing demand.”

“Elevated mortgage rates and high home prices continue to limit purchasing power, and the outlook for new home sales remains sensitive to financing costs and broader economic conditions,” she continued.

Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant noted that as mortgage rates remain near a three-year high, “the new home industry is experiencing the same pullback in demand that we are seeing on the resale side.”

“While home builders can help offset some of the pain of higher rates by offering buyers rate buydowns and favorable financing, prospective buyers are cautious as we head into the end of 2026,” she continued. “Some buyers have been priced out of the market, while others are simply waiting until 2027, hoping for more favorable conditions.”

Inventory remained on the downslope, falling 1.5% month-over-month and 4.1% year-over-year to 477,000. At the current sales rate, this clocked in at an eight-month supply, down 14% from last month and 11.1% year-over-year.

Builder activity has been significantly diminished due to aforementioned market challenges, with builder confidence recently tanking to a 14-year low.

“Builders are responding with incentives and pricing adjustments, but a more sustained improvement in affordability will be important for strengthening housing demand,” noted NAHB Chairman Bill Owens.

In line with this trend, the median price for a new home slipped 0.3% month-over-month and 3.2 year-over-year to $391,300. Sturtevant noted that this was near a “five year low.”

“Traditionally, new homes command a premium over existing homes, but in October, the median price of a new home was 6% lower than the median price of an existing home,” she continued.”

Sturtevant concluded that with incentives and lower pricing on the table, “new homes continue to be an attractive option for buyers who remain in the market, particularly when builders can offer a discounted interest rate.”

She noted, though, that the issue at hand is “that there are simply fewer buyers in the market as we head into the last few weeks of the year.”

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

Homebuyers are gaining leverage across much of the country, but assuming every seller is ready to accept a discount could leave them misreading their local market. Read more.

#5444. Oatey Raises Record $437,609 for Cancer Research

During this year’s Bike to Cure weekend, 170 Oatey associates from locations around the world came together to ride, volunteer, and raise funds for cancer research at Cleveland Clinic.

Oatey has raised a company-record $437,609 through its 2026 VeloSano campaign, bringing its cumulative fundraising for cancer research to more than $2.1 million.

The plumbing products manufacturer finished as the second-highest fundraising team in this year’s campaign. Over 11 years of participation, funds raised through Oatey have supported 21 cancer research projects at Cleveland Clinic.

The milestone comes as VeloSano, a global fundraising movement supporting cancer research at Cleveland Clinic, surpassed $115 million raised since its launch in 2014. According to the organization, 100% of funds raised go directly toward cancer research.

“Surpassing $115 million in fundraising is an extraordinary accomplishment, but what is even more meaningful is the innovative research and scientific progress those dollars are making possible,” Oatey CEO Neal Restivo said. “We are proud to play a part in its success and deeply grateful to everyone who makes this work possible.”

During VeloSano’s Bike to Cure weekend Sept. 18 to 19, 170 Oatey employees from locations around the world participated by riding, volunteering, and raising money. Cyclists completed routes of up to 100 miles, while others participated virtually or supported riders at the company’s sponsored rest stop.

The fundraising movement has become a significant part of Oatey’s community engagement efforts, with employees, families, and industry partners participating in campaigns throughout the year. VeloSano previously recognized the company with its All In Award in 2021.

#5443. Fischer Homes Surpasses $39M Raised for St. Jude

The St. Louis Dream Home built by Fischer Homes.

Fischer Homes helped raise $4.06 million for St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital through its 2026 St. Jude Dream Home Giveaway campaigns in Cincinnati, St. Louis, and Louisville.

The campaigns coincided with Fischer Homes marking 20 years of partnership with St. Jude and brought the builder’s cumulative contributions to more than $39.36 million. The 2026 Cincinnati campaign generated $1.48 million, St. Louis raised $1.68 million, and Louisville contributed $900,000.

Fischer Homes designed and built a Dream Home for each market, making it the only builder to construct three St. Jude Dream Homes in a single year, they noted. The homes included a Linden plan in Cincinnati valued at $540,000, an Emmett plan in St. Louis valued at $735,000, and a Grandin plan in Louisville valued at $533,000.

Trade partners, vendors, sponsors, employees, and community members contributed materials, labor, and other resources to complete the homes and support the giveaways.

“When we look back on 20 years with St. Jude, we’re reminded that the impact of this partnership goes far beyond the homes we’ve built or the dollars we’ve raised,” Fischer Homes said in announcing the milestone. “It’s about the lasting difference made possible by our associates, trade partners, vendors, and local supporters, who have contributed their time, talent, and resources to a mission that matters.”

In recognition of its support, Fischer Homes received a St. Jude 20-Year Partnership Award at the 2026 St. Jude Dream Home Builder Summit in Memphis. The builder constructed its first St. Jude Dream Home in Cincinnati in 2003.

The St. Jude Dream Home Giveaway raises money through giveaways of newly constructed homes, with builders and their trade partners donating time, materials, and resources to support St. Jude’s childhood cancer and other disease research and treatment efforts.

#5441. The Hearthstone BUILDER Humanitarian Award Continues Its Legacy

Close to three decades ago, Hearthstone and BUILDER joined forces to create an annual award that recognizes home builders who are dedicated to giving back and making a difference in their communities. For upcoming 2027, the Hearthstone BUILDER Humanitarian Award will honor its 28th inductee.

Since its inception in 1999, the award has highlighted numerous home building icons, from David Weekley to Larry Webb, and organizations, like Lennar Corp. and Meritage Homes, for demonstrating a lifetime commitment to public service and has contributed close to $8 million to various deserving charities.

The 2027 winner will be recognized during an in-person awards ceremony at the Builder 100 Leadership Summit, taking place May 3 to 5 in Dana Point, California.

Before the announcement next year, let’s reflect on some of the organizations and humanitarians we’ve celebrated in the past five years.

2026: Allan Merrill of Beazer Homes earned the Hearthstone honor in 2026. What began with a single race by Merrill has since expanded into a company-wide model of giving, anchored by a national nonprofit partnership with the Fisher House Foundation, sustained funding, and employee participation and pride.

2025: The Lennar Foundation, the charitable arm of Lennar Corp., was awarded in 2025. Created in 1989 to give back to the communities in which Lennar builds, the foundation has focused on many causes including helping veterans transition to civilian life, offering job training to formerly incarcerated individuals, funding life-saving medical research, and more.

2024: Pat Neal was recognized in 2024 for his dedication to land preservation in his home state of Florida. During his development career, the founder and chairman of Neal Communities has balanced developing land for homes and preserving it for future generations.

2023: Recognized as a collective company, Meritage Homes has supported countless charitable causes in its 40-year history. Guided by its core value of “start with heart,” Meritage and its employees have contributed charitable funds and volunteer hours to support No Child Hungry, Operation Homefront, Arbor Day Foundation, and more.

2022: As a fourth-generation home builder, HistoryMaker Homes CEO Nelson Mitchell has a servant heart that has been passed down through generations. Under Mitchell’s leadership, HistoryMaker has raised more than $14 million dollars for children with disabilities, impoverished communities, veterans, and the homeless.

2021: Taylor Morrison’s chairman and CEO Sheryl Palmer fosters a workplace that continually gives back. The company’s employee-value proposition, called TMLiving, includes daily huddles that allow employees to have regular conversations about everyone’s charitable efforts and provide inspiring examples of how team members give back to their communities.

2021: Edward Burr, the CEO of GreenPointe Holdings, started the Monique Burr Foundation for Children, an after-school program designed to educate and empower children against abuse, bullying and victimization, in honor of his late wife. The foundation has educated more than 5 million children in Florida.

#5440. Epochal launches with $100M to help developers train predictive AI models

Artificial intelligence tooling startup Epochal AI Inc. launched today with $100 million in funding.

The capital was provided by Chief Executive Officer Guodong Zhang, a machine learning researcher who earlier co-founded xAI Corp. He established Epochal earlier this year with two other xAI co-founders, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss. The company’s staff also includes former researchers from Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC and Google DeepMind.

Epochal’s first offering is a cloud service called the Epochal Time Portal. According to the company, it enables developers to train AI models that can predict future events. The service does so by providing models with access to historical web data from the past 30 years.

If a bank wishes to train an AI that can predict quarterly earnings, it could use the service to fetch financial results from the first three quarters of 2025. It could then ask the AI to estimate fourth-quarter results from the same year.

After the model generates its predictions, developers can compare them against real fourth-quarter earnings to check the model’s accuracy. They can make adjustments if necessary and then repeat the training workflow until the model starts generating accurate forecasts.

The Epochal Time Portal features more than 1 trillion historical web pages on launch. Each entry includes a timestamp that indicates when it was created. According to the company, its timestamps make it possible to track how a web page changed over time.

AI models access the content through a purpose-built search engine. It enables them to specify the time periods from which they wish to retrieve web pages. According to Epochal, its platform provides one-minute granularity for the most frequently updated pages.

Like consumer search engines, the Epochal Time Portal prioritizes the web pages that are most relevant to each given query. The difference is that it considers web pages’ creation date when evaluating relevance. If a query contains the term “Meta” but asks for pages created before 2021, the year Facebook Inc. rebranded, the Epochal Time Portal will not bring up pages that relate to the social networking giant.

Today’s frontier models can determine that they’re being trained on historical data rather than up-to-date information. For example, a model might compare the creation date of a web page to the virtual clock of the operating system on which it deployed. Such discrepancies can lower the effectiveness of training runs.

According to Epochal, its service mitigates the issue by deploying AI models in sandboxes synced to their training data. If a company is training a model on we pages from 2025, the Epochal Time Portal will run it on a Linux version from that year. It applies the same precautions to the software tools and programming language versions that models use.

The Epochal Time Portal is initially available in a single free tier with low usage limits. Epochal plans to follow up the launch by sharing the results of several AI experiments that its researchers have carried out using the service.
