#5402. Zoom’s conversations-to-completion strategy is starting to pay off

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

Zoom Communications Inc. has spent the better part of the past few years building products to become more than just the video company everyone used during the pandemic. Its fiscal third-quarter results, posted Monday, showed the strategy is working, though more work remains.

Total revenue grew 4.9%, but enterprise revenue rose 8.6%, its fastest pace in 13 quarters. Zoom raised its full-year outlook and announced its first quarterly dividend of 25 cents per share.

The acceleration should be viewed not as a one-quarter anomaly but as a manifestation of the strategy the company outlined at Zoomtopia about a month ago – moving from “conversations to completion.” That strategy gives customers a reason to buy more of Zoom and builds a competitive moat wider than most investors realize.

The concept of conversations to completion has enough merit that Microsoft used those exact words at its recent Ignite 2026 event. In fact, it held an entire session on the topic. Though having an 800-pound gorilla like Microsoft jump on a trend might seem threatening, Zoom has a significant lead and can use Microsoft’s marketing to add momentum to its current tailwind.

Nearly all work starts with a conversation: a meeting, a call, a chat thread or a customer interaction. Then everyone leaves, and the real work begins: updating the customer record, writing the follow-up and scheduling the next step. Collaboration vendors have always owned the first step, leaving the second to someone else.

Zoom wants both. “We’d like to leverage AI to transform our business from a conversation-centric vendor to a system of completions,” Chief Executive Eric Yuan said on the earnings call. He later put it more plainly: “Conversation is step 1. Step 2, AI will take over.”

His proof point was Zoom’s own sales organization, which uses ZoomMate, the company’s agentic framework. Sellers, Yuan said, “no longer log into the backend CRM system.” The agent takes over after the call ends. In enterprise software, value is shifting from where work is recorded to where it originates.

AI agents are quickly becoming a commodity, and so are the models behind them. What is scarce is context, the knowledge of what was decided, by whom, and why. Zoom sits on the richest source of it in most companies: what people actually said to one another and to customers.

“Any agent without context really cannot get work done,” Yuan said. That’s why the unified context layer Zoom showcased at Zoomtopia is central to the story. It links conversations to chats, documents and third-party systems, ensuring people and agents work from the same information.

My Notes, the company’s AI note-taker, extends that reach to third-party and in-person conversations. Yuan said it is nearing 2 million monthly active users, with one financial services firm rolling it out to 80,000 wealth advisers. Chief Financial Officer Michelle Chang added that online customers using My Notes have been associated with a 50% reduction in churn.

That is what will create a deeper competitive moat for Zoom. The more context a customer stores with Zoom, the more useful its agents become and the harder it is to leave. Zoom’s moat is not the meeting. Think of it as the memory of the meeting.

A context layer is only as good as the number of conversations it ingests, and this is where Zoom’s breadth of platforms matters. Meetings, phone, chat, contact center and now sales intelligence all feed into the same foundation, and each product gets smarter from the others.

Customers are consolidating. DSI Systems is replacing five separate products with Zoom. SolarWinds expanded its Zoom licenses while “recalibrating its Microsoft package,” according to Yuan. Enterprise net dollar expansion returned to 100%, its highest level in 11 quarters. “Strong RPO growth reflects our continued success in landing larger, longer-term multiproduct platform deals, demonstrating growing demand for our AI-first platform,” Chang said.

Customer experience is where completion gets paid for. Zoom CX recurring revenue grew in the high double digits for the seventh straight quarter, and all 10 of its largest CX deals included paid AI. More telling, Zoom said at Zoomtopia that 90% of its top 100 CX deals in the first half were with customers new to Zoom. Contact center is no longer a cross-sell. It is a front door.

Chang described the differentiation as “the ability to think about customer experience in a whole and fresh new way.” Specifically, she said, “to be able to seamlessly hand off from virtual agents to agents assisted with AI is a big winner for us.” AI-native startups have the virtual agent but not the human side. Legacy contact center vendors have the humans but not the pace of innovation. Zoom has both on one platform.

There is also an economic moat. Zoom runs most of its AI workload on its own small models and saves the expensive frontier models for harder tasks. “I fundamentally believe no single model can satisfy everything,” Yuan said. Gross margin rose even as AI usage grew, a feat that a point product reselling another company’s tokens cannot easily match.

The quarter was strong, but analyst questions revealed several concerns.

Some will read the dividend as a sign of maturity. With more than $7 billion in cash and free cash flow margins above 40%, I see a company that can fund innovation and return capital at the same time.

Although these issues came up during the call, most of the investment community remains positive about Zoom. In his note, Arun Bhatia of William Blair wrote, “Churn and downsell rates are becoming more favorable, AI usage and monetization are increasing, and adoption of new products such as Phone and Zoom CX is strong. We are encouraged by these trends and see potential for a growth uptick in the future.”

Zoom’s headline growth resembles that of a mature software vendor, but the company is in transition, so it’s important to look beyond the numbers. The underlying enterprise business is built to be a platform that uses context to drive customers toward more products and longer commitments. Investors should watch enterprise growth, net expansion and CX AI attach rates rather than the top line.

For information technology and business leaders, the lesson extends beyond Zoom. Conversation data is a strategic asset, so decide deliberately where it lives and which agents can act on it. Insist on openness so that context can feed the tools you choose. Start where completion is easy to measure, in the contact center and in sales.

That is where Zoom is proving that the conversation was never the product. The outcome is.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5400. A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he said.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A big part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” said Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively new sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he said, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move quickly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

What you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he said.

But you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

Often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré said. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

But that can be a long road. Sangaré said it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

And when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré said; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

#5398. Amazon’s $18B bet on Anthropic tops $200B, for a moment, in the Claude maker’s historic market debut

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old company was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

#5397. CoStar photographers say quotas rose, now some want to unionize

CoStar architectural photographers are exploring unionizing with IBEW, citing unmanageable quotas, travel, and job security concerns. CoStar says point changes reflect outsourced editing and automation, and warns unionization could add costs and reduce flexibility.  AI Summary

Earlier this fall, CoStar Group hosted its first Global Photography Conference in Richmond, Virginia. The event, which was held at the firm’s new Foundry Park campus, was largely lauded as a success by CoStar and even members of its photography team.

CoStar CEO Andy Florance, also celebrated what appeared to be a successful event, writing in a post on LinkedIn that the team set the standard “for future collaboration as they shared techniques, tested new ideas and innovated what’s next for visual storytelling in real estate.”

“I’m excited to see what they continue to build, one image at a time,” Florance, a HousingWire Vanguard, added.

But under the surface, sources that spoke with HousingWire said that things within the listing portal giant’s photography team are not as hunky-dory as the social media posts paint them out to be. Over the past few weeks HousingWire has spoken with several sources within CoStar about a recent unionization effort among the company’s architectural photographers, which were the photographers behind the content used for the Homes.com Neighborhood Guides.

The sources, who asked for anonymity due to fear of retribution, claim that the workload for architectural photographers is “unmanageable” and “impossible to complete within the working hours.” In 2025, CoStar raised daily quotas for architectural photographers, which was followed by a move this September to lower the point value of assignments, which means, according to the sources, that photographers have to do more work each day to meet their minimum quotas.

Last year, work quotas were raised from 0.8 per day to 1.0 per day and the point value of different tiers was dropped from 1 point to  0.75 point  for Diamond, from 0.75 point  to 0.50 point for Platinum and from 0.50 point to 0.25 point for Gold. This means that, in the past, photographers could complete one Diamond project and meet their daily quota, but now they have to do one Diamond project and one Gold project to meet quota.

Sources also claimed that there is no work-life balance as they sometimes have to drive over an hour to go to and from appointments and that it takes well over an hour to upload the images captured that day.

However, sources did note that CoStar has outsourced the photo editing work to help offset some of these issues, which the company confirmed.

Despite this shift in responsibilities, the sources said all of these challenges have been compounded by layoffs creating shortages of architectural photographers across the country. Sources said that this sometimes requires them to travel far outside their normal service areas further increasing drive times.

“Not only did they bump up the daily requirement by 25%, they also scrapped any sort of flexible scheduling. Now every single photographer is expected to be on-call 12 hours a day, Monday through Friday. No exceptions. This change came [out of] nowhere,” a user named richmondrefugee posted in a subreddit called r/RealEstatePhotography. “And if that wasn’t enough, today they let go of two dozen folks — just like that. It’s been a mess, y’all.”

In addition to this, the sources said they are concerned for their job security as the company continues to cut the architectural photography staff while hiring residential photographers. This is a more entry-level position at CoStar and as such these photographers are compensated at a lower rate. Sources within the company said that these other photographers were brought in to do Matterports, but are being sent out to do assignments that architectural photographers have done in the past.

“They had me train my replacement! I was getting paid six figures and one day they asked me to train this “Matterport Photographer,” making $40K. So I spent the week with him training. One day I was at his trunk when he was getting his Matterport and saw his Costar bag with all the same gear as me. I said why are they giving a Matterport photographer over 10K in camera equipment. A month later I was gone and they have him doing my job,” KeepitMelloOoW posted in the r/RealEstatePhotogrpahy subreddit.

Sources told HousingWire that these concerns about job security, work load and work-life balance are what prompted the architectural photography team to explore the idea of unionizing by joining the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW). This resulted in a link to an IBEW unionization interest form being circulated within CoStar.

Unsurprisingly, the link caught the attention of CoStar management. In response to the link, Lisa Ruggles, CoStar’s senior vice president of global operations sent an email to all of the firm’s photographers that was obtained by HousingWire and verified by CoStar, in which she said that CoStar was “was surprised to hear of an anonymous email afterward urging Architectural Photographers to join the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers,” in light of the success of the Global Photography Conference.

According to the email, “media shoots” are the “top priority” for the firm’s architectural photography team and that the point values for assignment changed due to the outsourcing of editing and post-production of images.

“Photo retouching now goes to a dedicated resource, while Matterport and floor-plan uploads are automated —removing tasks photographers once handled. We must use new technology to compete. A union cannot change the work our customers demand or our business requires,” Ruggles wrote.

Ruggles also noted that the change in point values also helped level the playing field and make sure all photographers from across the company were completing the same level of work. She also said that CoStar is monitoring how long it takes photographers to complete various projects and adjusting their value.

“We are building a dynamic system to better account for longer trips in rural markets,” the email stated. “Outside of the news and media industries, we know of no company that directly employs as many photographers as CoStar. We want to preserve as many of these well-compensated positions as possible because they provide meaningful work, competitive benefits, and financial stability for employees and their families — but the business must remain economically sustainable.”

Ruggles added that CoStar feels unionization would make it harder for the company to respond to market pressures and shifts in business needs, which would not be in the best interests of employees. Additionally, Ruggles wrote that an IBEW election victory would bind all employees in the bargaining unit to a negotiated contract, and that a customary dues provision could require payments of 2% of pay, with opt-outs unavailable in most states where it operates. The company said employment terms could improve, stay the same or decline through bargaining and urges employees to make an informed decision, noting that unions are usually difficult to remove once elected.

Sources within CoStar, as well as the company itself, have confirmed that no formal reply regarding Ruggles’ email has been sent. Despite this, sources told HousingWire that the unionization effort is continuing to proceed.

CoStar did not wish to share any additional comments regarding the unionization effort.

#5396. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”

When I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5395. Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious plan to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid quickly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

“I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”

For Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he said. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

“I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd said. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”

“You can tell,” he said, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd said he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The company now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

“This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

#5394. Egan-Jones Notes Higher Borrowing Costs Alongside Steady Credit Fundamentals

NEW YORK, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Egan-Jones released its November 2026 review of US credit conditions, finding that borrowing costs sit well above year-ago levels while corporate and consumer credit quality has held up. The review attributes most of the increase to higher Treasury yields, with wider spreads adding to it.

The 5-year Treasury yielded 4.59% on 5 November 2026, against 3.76% a year earlier. Spreads, the extra yield investors require over Treasuries, widened as well: BB-rated spreads reached 213 basis points on 5 November, their widest since March, and BBB spreads stood at 116.

Credit fundamentals have not followed. Median interest coverage, which measures earnings against interest expense, stands at 11.4x across 404 issuers on their latest filings, and the June quarter-end median of 10.3x was the highest since 2023. Leverage trends divide by sector, with 48% of covered real estate issuers improving while 53% of energy issuers worsened, even as oil and gas ranks strongest on the firm's measure of credit momentum.

Consumer credit has also improved. Credit-card delinquencies fell for an eighth consecutive quarter, to 2.85%, and unemployment, at 4.1% in October, is below its 4.5% peak of November 2025. Collateral prices are mixed, with commercial property up 8.8% and homes 3.0% over the year while used cars and apartments are down. After an allowance for delinquencies, Egan-Jones calculates, a new-car loan now yields less than a 30-year mortgage.

The review finds how Egan-Jones ratings have performed over the longer record. Across issuer groups formed each year from 2000 to 2025, recorded default rates on the firm's unsolicited ratings, made from public information with no issuer fee, sit below the published rates of two legacy agencies at investment and speculative grade and at one, five and ten years, though Egan-Jones cautions that the three may not define default the same way.

In every year from 2015 to 2025, other agencies' rating actions moved toward the Egan-Jones rating on the same issuer at least three times in four.

#5393. So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm

Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Microsoft says the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

The offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

All of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in new hires.

The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the company decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a company right now?

Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

But it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one company.

“It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.”

Hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more important than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

The jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual company. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software company.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.

Software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue quickly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

The bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

One venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

1) Think VERY big, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a company that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

There are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

Whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Big Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a new role, a company of their own or a year with their family.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5392. Mortgage applications rise 6.1% even as 30-year hits 7.38%

MBA reported mortgage applications rose 6.1% for the week ending Nov. 20, 2026. Purchase activity led with a 10% gain, while the 30-year fixed rate averaged 7.38% and ARM share increased to 11.5%.  AI Summary

Mortgage applications increased 6.1% from one week earlier, according to data from the Mortgage Bankers Association’s (MBA) weekly mortgage applications survey for the week ending November 20, 2026.

On an unadjusted basis, the Index increased 3% compared with the previous week.

The refinance index increased 1% from the previous week and was 51% lower than the same week one year ago. The seasonally adjusted purchase index increased 10% from one week earlier. The unadjusted purchase index increased 5% compared with the previous week and was 16% lower than the same week one year ago.

“Mortgage rates moved higher, with the 30-year fixed rate rising to 7.38%, its highest level in five weeks. While mortgage rates increased slightly on a weekly average basis, rates declined over the course of the week, which likely spurred purchase application activity,” said Joel Kan, CMB, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist. “Purchase applications reached their strongest weekly pace since September but remained well behind last year’s pace.”

Kan added that a larger share of borrowers gravitated to ARM loans. The ARM share of activity accounted for 11.5% of applications, the highest share in more than a year, Kan noted.

“At 6.39%, the ARM mortgage rate was nearly a full percentage lower than the 30-year fixed rate last week. Refinance activity was flat over the week with conventional applications showing a small increase while VA refinances dropped more than 11%,” he said.

The refinance share of mortgage activity decreased to 40.1% of total applications from 41.1% the previous week. The adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) share of activity increased to 11.5% of total applications.

By product, the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) share of total applications decreased to 15.9% from 16.1% the week prior. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) share decreased to 12.4% from 12.8% the week prior. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) share of total applications remained unchanged at 0.5% from the week prior.

The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances ($832,750 or less) increased to 7.38% from 7.35%. Meanwhile, the average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with jumbo loan balances decreased to 7.29% from 7.31%.

The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages backed by the FHA decreased to 7.05% from 7.06% while rates for 15-year fixed-rate mortgages increased to 6.79% from 6.64%. The average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs slightly increased to 6.39% from 6.38%.

Xactus’s Mortgage Intent Index — which analyzes aggregated, anonymized credit-pull activity across the Xactus Intelligent Verification Platform — increased week-over-week to a reading of 97.8.

“Mortgage intent edged up approximately 2.2% week over week,” said Thomas Lloyd, chief strategy officer at Xactus. “The uptick follows last week’s Veterans Day-suppressed reading, suggesting underlying borrower demand remains present even in a challenging rate environment.”

Lloyd continued, “Early readings from the Daily Xactus Mortgage Intent Index offer some cautious optimism heading into Thanksgiving week — Monday’s reading of 65.9 reflects expected seasonal softness, but the year-over-year gap of approximately 16.5% is a notable improvement from the roughly 25% deficit seen in recent weeks.”

#5391. Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”

#5390. As US Provider Organizations Accelerate Enterprise Imaging Adoption, Frost & Sullivan Measures How Much of the Market Has Reached True Enterprise Imaging

Frost & Sullivan's Next-Generation Enterprise Imaging Framework, built on provider and vendor interviews, sets out what True Enterprise Imaging requires, released ahead of RSNA 2026

CUPERTINO, Calif., Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Provider organizations across the US are accelerating their move to enterprise imaging. The harder question is how many have reached the ideal state of enterprise imaging that so many vendors are talking about in the market today: a strategic platform of integrated capabilities to manage, access and use medical imaging across the full clinical enterprise. Health systems, academic medical centers, community hospitals, radiology groups and ambulatory providers now treat their imaging platform as the way to optimally image-enable the enterprise, with clinical, IT and executive leadership sharing the decision.

Enterprise Imaging, US, 2025â2030, a new study from the Healthcare & Life Sciences team at Frost & Sullivan, examines that shift from both sides of the market. It builds on more than a decade of Frost & Sullivan imaging informatics analysis that helped define enterprise imaging, and introduces the Frost & Sullivan Next-Generation Enterprise Imaging Framework, which sets out what that ideal platform state requires and what separates it from departmental PACS strategies. The study defines enterprise imaging by strategy and governance across specialties, not by the use of a single vendor.

A 360-Degree View of US Enterprise Imaging

The study is built on primary interviews on both sides of the market. Enterprise imaging purchasing decision-makers, including CIOs, CMIOs and Chairs of Radiology, were interviewed in each provider segment, alongside interviews across the majority of the enterprise imaging vendor community and ecosystem participants. Both are tied to a top-down/bottom-up market and maturity model by provider segment, following the practices used in Frost & Sullivan complex addressable market models. The approach brings together Frost & Sullivan's syndicated market analysis and Voice of Customer methods.

"The central issue in enterprise imaging is managing complexity at enterprise scale, across multi-site, multi-vendor and multi-ology environments," said Daniel Ruppar, Consulting Director, Healthcare & Life Sciences at Frost & Sullivan. "Providers are moving toward governed platforms that bring radiology, cardiology, pathology and the other -ologies together. Vendors that reduce fragmentation, support interoperability and improve workforce efficiency are best placed to support that move."

AI Moves From the Algorithm to the Enterprise

Frost & Sullivan establishes AI Orchestration & Governance as a new area within enterprise imaging, covering dedicated AI orchestration, governance and developer tooling delivered through the enterprise imaging platform. This is a key step for enterprise imaging market intelligence, and an early new definition as Frost & Sullivan continues to support the enterprise imaging industry. The question for providers is less about any single algorithm and more about how they best run AI across the enterprise: which models run where, how they are governed and who is accountable for them. Provider leaders also expect clearer financial evidence of return before they approve AI investment, not only qualitative impact cases.

Frost & Sullivan maps which provider segments are moving fastest into enterprise imaging and examines cloud, AI and reporting as the hot technology topics in the market.

"The decision in front of most provider organizations is no longer whether to move to an enterprise platform. It is how to get there and which partners can support the move," Ruppar added. "We listened to the market and built what it asked for: interviews across every provider segment, a maturity estimate for each segment and a clearer way to tell vendors apart, which providers asked for too. Many teams juggle several sources with no single source of truth. This study gives vendors and provider leaders the same independent picture of where the market is heading."

Frost & Sullivan's Healthcare & Life Sciences team will be at RSNA 2026, held at McCormick Place in Chicago from 29 November to 3 December. Frost & Sullivan is available to brief media, vendors and provider organizations on the findings and on what the move to governed, multi-ology platforms means for each.

To request more information on the study, visit www.frost.com/enterprise-imaging-2030.html.

Through Growth Pipeline as a Service, the company provides transformational strategies and best-practice models to identify, prioritize and realize growth opportunities.

#5389. Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm

Amazon and New York City are fighting again.

The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

On Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

In a blog post, Amazon said it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the company wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”

Amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel said. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The company also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

The standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled plans to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its plans for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most New Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6

City leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” said Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

Amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The company said it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in New York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

Meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

#5388. Formal verification startup Sequent raises $2.2M to prove code obeys its safety rules

Formal verification startup Sequent Inc. today announced that it has raised $2.2 million in new funding to take its Alan proof platform out of early access.

Founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set. Decentralized exchange Curve Finance is its first paying customer.

Curve also figures in how Sequent got started. Chief Executive Charles Cooper, who leads development of Vyper, one of the two main programming languages for Ethereum, inadvertently introduced a flaw into the Vyper compiler in 2021. Though the bug was fixed within months, programs already running on the blockchain could not be updated, leaving older Curve pools and other projects exposed when attackers used the flaw to take more than $50 million in July 2023.

Following the incident, Ramana Kumar, now Sequent’s chief technology officer and formerly an AI safety researcher at Google DeepMind, offered to help prove the Vyper compiler correct. Kumar co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct all the way down to the instructions a computer runs.

Cooper believes the lesson reaches far beyond crypto, saying that “smart contracts taught us that anything that can be exploited will be.” Banks, governments and companies running older systems have relied on keeping their code private, according to Cooper, who said AI-powered cyberattacks are now eroding that protection.

Alan works today on Vyper smart contracts, with support for Solidity and Solana in development and general software in Rust, C, TypeScript and Python to follow.

For now, engineers using Alan write rules for their code such as “no user can withdraw more than their balance” in plain language, and the job of finding a mathematical proof is handed to AI. Nothing the AI comes up with is taken on trust, as each proof has to get through HOL4, a checker Kumar has helped build for more than a decade.

For two-coin StableSwap pools holding standard tokens, Alan was used to prove that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order. The work also found minor accounting and rounding errors, none of which breached the limit. The founders are now proving the Vyper compiler itself, since the Curve proof does not cover the compiler where the 2021 flaw sat.

Along with AI computing costs, the funding will pay for engineering, sales and marketing hires. Subscriptions to Alan start at $99 a month for individuals, with auditor plans priced at $200 a month and team plans starting at $500 a month.

Frachtis and Metaplanet Holdings OÜ co-led the pre-seed round. Metaplanet is the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic PBC’s Series A round in 2021. According to Frachtis founder Xavier Meegan, crypto is the right place to start, with “billions already at risk.”

#5387. Epique’s ‘Power Agent’ trademark fight could put its branding at risk

Darryl Davis Seminars and Darryl Davis will face Epique Realty in SDNY next week over alleged POWER AGENT® trademark infringement. The court will hear a preliminary injunction motion as Epique presses counterclaims over “power” related marks.  AI Summary

Darryl Davis Seminars Inc.’s multi-million dollar federal trademark infringement lawsuit against Epique Realty, which accuses the virtual brokerage of unlawfully using the POWER AGENT® brand in its nationwide operations, is headed to court next week.

During the first week of December, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York will hold a hearing on a motion for a preliminary injunction filed by Darryl Davis and his firm that would bar Epique Realty, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, from using the POWER AGENT trademark.

Originally filed in late June, the lawsuit alleges that Houston-based Epique Realty adopted the POWER AGENT name and “built an entire brand architecture around it” despite being put on notice and asked to stop, according to the announcement. In addition to Epique Realty, the lawsuit also lists Joshua Miller, Janice Delcid, Christopher Miller, XYZ Corps 1-10 and John and Jane Does 1-10 as defendants.

Darryl Davis Seminars says it has used the POWER AGENT mark continuously since 1993 through The POWER Program, which it describes as the real estate industry’s oldest and longest-running agent training and coaching platform.

“POWER AGENT® has been our name since 1993, and both it and THE POWER PROGRAM® are registered trademarks,” Davis told HousingWire. “The law expects a trademark owner to protect its marks. We have for decades, and we will keep doing so. Because the matter is pending, I will let our court filings speak to the rest.”

In October, Epique filed a counterclaim asking for a ruling from the court that Davis’s trademark registrations of Power Agent programs do not give his firm exclusive rights to the word “power” and that this does not give Davis or his company the rights to a family of “Power” trademarks. Epique is also asking the court to force Davis and his firm to prove likely confusing for each expression of “Power” Epique was accused of. Epique is also seeking rulings from the court that its current uses of PowerFlex and PowerCon, do not infringe on Davis’s trademarks and that it is not liable “merely because an independently controlled agent or third party used POWER-formative wording.”

Epique emphasized in the filing that its agents are independent contractors and that the company does not hold passwords for agents’ personal social media accounts in order to edit or delete content, nor does it review agents’ social media posts or websites before they are published. This contradicts Davis’s complaint, which alleges that the brokerage’s independent contractor agreement requires agents to submit marketing or advertising posts for approval prior to publication. Additionally, the company said that under state law in Texas, where Epique is headquartered, the firm is only responsible for ensuring that advertising content produced by agents complies with state rules.

In a filing earlier this month, Davis largely denied Epique’s counterclaims, namely that he is trying to trademark the word “Power” by itself and he and his firm rejected Epique’s request that the court declares that Darryl Davis Seminars does not own the word “power” exclusively and that it does not have an across-the-board monopoly over trademarks containing the word. Throughout the filing, Davis maintained that Epique infringed on his firm’s trademarks and he asked the court to reject Epique’s counter claims.

This news was first reported by Inman. Epique Realty did not immediately returned HousingWire’s request for comment.

#5385. Yazan Al Homsi-Backed Aduro and Rocket Doctor AI Announce Pilot, Network and Study Milestones

Aduro targets a third-quarter 2027 finish for its life cycle study, and the pharmacy pilot is set for a 90-day evaluation

VANCOUVER, BC, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Aduro Clean Technologies said in November that it had engaged Delphi to advance a comparative life cycle assessment of its Hydrochemolytic Technology. Vancouver-based Rocket Doctor AI Inc. said its physicians joined the Altais network in California and that it launched a 90-day pharmacy pilot in Canada. Investor Yazan Al Homsi holds a position in both companies.

On Nov. 17, Aduro, based in London, Ontario, said it had engaged Delphi, a Canadian sustainability consultancy, for the next phase of its life cycle assessment program. The study will use operating data from Aduro's Next Generation Process Pilot Plant and follow ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 standards. Three independent experts will review it. It will compare Hydrochemolytic Technology, a water-based process for recycling waste plastics and upgrading heavy oils, with pyrolysis. Aduro is targeting completion in the third quarter of 2027.

On Nov. 11, Rocket Doctor AI said that Rocket Doctor Practice Group, P.C., an affiliated professional corporation, had joined the Altais network. The move adds primary care physicians and specialists for eligible patients in California. Altais is a clinical services company that supports physicians and care teams.

On Nov. 18, Rocket Doctor AI announced that its subsidiary, Rocket Doctor Inc., had begun a 90-day pilot with a Canadian pharmacy chain. The pilot offers physician-led virtual care at 25 pharmacy locations in Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario. The pilot launched in October. The chain, which has not been named, will review each location against utilization, engagement, commercial results and other agreed criteria before deciding whether to expand.

Al Homsi invests in clean technology and AI-enabled healthcare.

Statements about the Aduro study's completion, the pharmacy pilot's evaluation and any expansion are forward-looking and depend on the companies' own timelines and decisions.

Aduro Clean Technologies, based in London, Ontario, develops patented water-based technologies that chemically recycle waste plastics, upgrade heavy crude and bitumen into lighter oil, and convert renewable oils into higher-value fuels or renewable chemicals. The company says its Hydrochemolytic Technology uses water as the reactive agent and runs at relatively low temperatures and cost.

Rocket Doctor AI Inc., based in Vancouver, develops physician-built, AI-powered healthcare tools. Its subsidiary, Rocket Doctor Inc., operates a digital health platform and marketplace that lets physicians launch and manage their own virtual or hybrid practices. The company says more than 350 physicians have provided care through its platform across more than 800,000 patient visits.

Yazan Al Homsi is a UAE-based investor and managing partner of Catalyst Communications DMCC, which he founded in Dubai in 2018. He was previously based in Vancouver, where he founded Founders Round Capital in 2017 and built a track record of investments in early-stage and small-cap companies. He earned a finance degree from McGill University in 2004 and holds the Chartered Financial Analyst designation. Before turning to investing, he spent more than a decade with PricewaterhouseCoopers in the Middle East, rising to director and focusing on transaction due diligence and valuation.

#5384. RBC Signals brings in $10M investment to expand strategic frontiers for satellite services

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 6:33 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 6:33 pm

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has announced a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the company’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

In August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals announced a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace.

The newly announced investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners, a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report.

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, said today in a news release.

“By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith said. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”

Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the company’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas said.
