#5371. How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am

It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

Now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

The disastrous update that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

No. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

The question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the company has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella said, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

Some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Plan) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

Full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a company partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in big, big trouble.

Since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.)

Over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

What happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the company with reports.

The first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

Most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from new finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

Moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

No surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on a deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and others aren’t built to process.

Since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

Meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

In theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

Microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple users to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

More broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

The cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to issue OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

OOBs are important enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security issue involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he said, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”

Think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

Managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

It’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

What needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

It’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5370. Better signs agreement with mortgage servicer to grow HELOC volume

Better signed an agreement with an unnamed mortgage servicer to offer HELOCs and home equity loans to existing borrowers. The Week 7 scorecard also reported $38.97M in annualized corporate savings since Nov. 17 as part of its $64.2M savings target.  AI Summary

Better Home & Finance Holding Co. signed an agreement with an unnamed mortgage servicer to offer home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and home equity loans to existing borrowers, expanding its lead-generation channels as the company continues its turnaround efforts.

The agreement, announced Tuesday in the company’s Week 7 Better 2.0 scorecard, is expected to provide a lower-cost customer acquisition channel.

Since its Week 6 scorecard on Nov. 17, Better has identified additional efficiencies across its corporate organization that are expected to generate a total of $38.97 million in annualized savings. The company also reported $770,000 in additional annualized savings from mortgage operations.

Better said it plans to pursue another $1.5 million in vendor-related reductions by Dec. 1. The company is working toward a broader cost savings target of $64.2 million.

“HELOC volume with our partners continues to grow each week, four more brokerages are lined up to join our wholesale platform, and two new partnerships are set to launch. At the same time, we’re moving toward a signed agreement to sell Birmingham Bank, which will let us focus fully on our U.S. business,” said Vishal Garg, Better’s founder and head of product, platform and innovation.

The company has received five term sheets for about $50 million in debt financing tied to the proposed sale of the bank and is continuing discussions with prospective financing partners.

The company said its AI-powered HELOC partnership with a large existing customer is live, with volume increasing weekly. Better is also preparing a multichannel campaign to expand the product through its wholesale platform and onboard additional brokerages.

Four more mortgage brokerages are in the pipeline to join the platform. Two previously announced partnerships — with a rental credit management platform and a home inspection company — are expected to launch early next week.

Better is also advancing discussions with three other major partners and a previously revived large-scale partnership, its release stated.

#5368. Startup Spotlight: An engineer’s search for better, safer baby products led him to launch Birch

Startup Spotlight profiles tech startups in the Pacific Northwest.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am

A new baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

“We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla said. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

To spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

Birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has issues with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and New Jersey.

Gangiredla said the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

If you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla said. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”

The platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for users.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch

Birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

The impossible research burden on new parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

How universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — big metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your company?

It’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

That “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

#5367. Colorado first responders can now get state home mortgage help

Colorado launched CHFA Colorado Champions to expand state housing help for first responders. The move follows similar homebuyer assistance efforts in states including Connecticut, Maryland, Texas, Florida and Tennessee.  AI Summary

A borrower earning nearly $197,000 a year usually doesn’t look like a typical candidate for state housing help. In Colorado, if that borrower is a firefighter, emergency medical technician or police officer, the person now qualifies.

The Colorado Housing and Finance Authority launched a homeownership program this month for first responders and law enforcement officers. CHFA Colorado Champions uses a new state law that raises income limits for eligible borrowers.

Colorado is among a growing list of states offering homebuying assistance to public-service workers. The goal is to give them more chances to live near where they serve. Maryland, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Texas, Florida and South Carolina also offer similar programs.

Earlier this month, Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont announced a new homeownership assistance program for first responders. It offers up to $25,000 in forgivable down payment and closing cost assistance. The program stems from a law Lamont signed this year.

“By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them,” Lamont said in a statement.

CHFA Colorado Champions arrives as the housing market weakens, following several years of zoning and regulatory reform.

Colorado’s single-family housing market has been steadily cooling since spring, according to HousingWire Intelligence data through Nov. 20. Inventory peaked in September and has barely eased, while median list prices have fallen since July. Homes are also taking longer to sell, with days on market rising since late July and price reductions staying elevated.

The latest weekly figures show no reversal, with single-family homes taking a median 91 days to sell, up from 84. The median single-family list price is $599,000, and about 48% of single-family listings carry price cuts, the data show.

Lawmakers have spent years trying to improve affordability, mostly by loosening local land-use rules. In 2024, Gov. Jared Polis signed laws requiring more density near transit and clearing the way for accessory dwelling units. The package also removed some parking minimums for urban multifamily housing and lifted limits on unrelated people living together.

A law Polis signed this year requires towns with more than 2,000 people to allow housing on certain small parcels. Eligible land belongs to school districts, colleges, transit districts, housing authorities and qualifying nonprofits. The law takes effect Dec. 31, 2027, while lot-size bills failed in the Legislature this year.

Senate Bill 26-053, a bipartisan law, raised CHFA’s mortgage income limits to 110% of standard guidelines. That allows eligible borrowers earning up to $196,810 a year to qualify.

The program offers a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage. The program covers down payment and closing costs up to the lesser of $25,000 or 4% of the first mortgage. Borrowers apply through a CHFA participating lender.

The aid is a second mortgage. Repayment is deferred until the term ends, the first mortgage is paid off, or the borrower sells, refinances or moves.

CHFA Executive Director Thomas Bryan said in a statement that first responders keep communities safe. Many can’t afford local homes, he added.

“They should be able to live where they serve,” Sen. Barbara Kirkmeyer, one of the law’s sponsors, said in a statement.

#5366. Johannesburg's Alchemi Pharmacy Credits Jocelyn Freimuth for Pharmacy Support

Alchemi CEO Zvi Sacks calls Jocelyn Freimuth "an invaluable partner" to the South African pharmacy and recommends her "without hesitation."

NASHVILLE, Tenn., Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Zvi Sacks, CEO of Alchemi Compounding Pharmacy in Johannesburg, South Africa, has credited Jocelyn Freimuth, PharmD, MBA, BSN, BCSCP, CEO of Camino Compass, with supporting his team on formulation development and troubleshooting.

Medicines sold in South Africa generally must be registered with the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority (SAHPRA), which must first be satisfied that each is safe, effective, and of good quality. Section 14(4) of the Medicines and Related Substances Act exempts medicines compounded for an individual patient, as a July analysis by Werksmans Attorneys outlines, leaving quality largely in the compounding pharmacist's hands. Sterile preparations raise the stakes, since most are injected or infused and leave no room for contamination.

Formulation development in sterile compounding means choosing the ingredients, concentrations, and containers that keep a preparation stable and sterile through its shelf life. Troubleshooting starts when something fails, from early degradation to a failed sterility test, and traces the problem back to its source in the process.

"Jocelyn's scientific depth and experience have been especially valuable in addressing the critical aspects of safety and sterility, which matter enormously in a sterile compounding environment," said Sacks.

"Compounding rules differ from one country to the next, but sterility does not," said Freimuth. "A preparation has to be right before it reaches the patient, and that is the standard I work to with every pharmacy, in the United States or abroad."

Alchemi is among the compounding pharmacies Freimuth supports outside the United States. Her international work also includes specialty pharmacy lectures at universities in Vietnam and a research presentation at the 25th Asian Conference on Clinical Pharmacy in Bangkok in July 2026.

For Sacks, how she works matters just as much. "Jocelyn is always willing to help, and she does it in a friendly, kind and approachable way," he said. "Her guidance is practical and reliable, and she makes complex problems feel manageable. We really enjoy working with her and would recommend her without hesitation."

About Jocelyn Freimuth and Camino Compass

Jocelyn Freimuth, PharmD, MBA, BSN, BCSCP, is a board-certified sterile compounding pharmacist and the Co-Founder and CEO of Camino Compass, a Nashville-based healthcare consulting and management firm. Drawing on more than 15 years across nursing, pharmacy, regulatory compliance, education, and healthcare executive leadership, she advises pharmacies, clinics, telehealth organizations, and medical providers in the United States and internationally. The firm's services include operational pharmacy support, regulatory compliance, accreditation support, healthcare education, startup and build-out consulting and team training. For more information, visit caminocompass.com or connect with her on LinkedIn.

Alchemi Compounding Pharmacy is based in Midrand, Johannesburg, in South Africa's Gauteng province. Led by CEO Zvi Sacks, the pharmacy prepares customized medications for medical practitioners, allied healthcare professionals, and their patients. For more information, visit alchemicompoundingpharmacy.co.za.

#5365. CPI vs. PCE: 5 differences between the two U.S. inflation gauges

CPI and PCE both measure U.S. inflation but differ on publisher, use, scope, weights and substitution. See 5 differences.

Anyone tracking U.S. inflation soon runs into two competing figures: CPI, the Consumer Price Index, and PCE, a price index for personal consumption expenditures. The two rarely match, and the Federal Reserve prefers PCE. A reader who checks only one of them could come away more worried, or less worried, than the other measure would justify. Any gap between them comes from deliberate choices, made by the people who build each measure, about what to count and how much each cost should matter.

The difference matters because each measure settles something real, and the two settle different things for different people. Fed officials judge their own record against an inflation target, so the reading they watch tells them whether they are succeeding. The yearly Social Security raise goes to about 75 million people, according to CNBC, and its size depends on an inflation index. When the two measures move apart, policymakers and retirees can be looking at different versions of the same year. Knowing which number a headline reports is therefore more than trivia. It tells a reader whose decision rests on that number.

The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland has laid out how the two main U.S. inflation gauges differ, from whose spending each one counts to how much weight housing carries and what happens to each gauge when shoppers trade down. On the latest core readings, PCE inflation ran at 3.3% through October 2026 and CPI inflation at 2.6% through September 2026. Those readings cover different months, but both sit above the Fed's 2% target. None of the differences between the gauges makes one measure right and the other wrong. Each choice suits a different job, which is why one economy can produce two honest readings.

The two gauges come from different agencies, with the Bureau of Labor Statistics producing the CPI and the Bureau of Economic Analysis producing PCE, according to a 2014 analysis by the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. BEA publishes PCE as part of its consumer spending data, so the Fed judges its own progress with a figure that another agency builds. The agency behind a number therefore matters. Two statistical agencies with their own methods can examine the same economy and report different results.

Separate agencies suggest two independent readings of prices, but the agencies do not work from separate raw material. BEA lists the Consumer Price Index, the Producer Price Index and the Consumer Expenditures Survey among its major sources for PCE, and all three are products of the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The gauge that usually appears beside the CPI is built partly from the CPI. When the two diverge, much of the gap can come from how each agency weighs and combines shared inputs, rather than from prices moving in one gauge and not in the other. A gap between CPI and PCE is a question about method first.

For most households, CPI is the inflation number that matters. In a 2014 analysis, the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland describes CPI as the gauge used to adjust Social Security payments and the one cited in news headlines. The CPI that sets a retiree's raise is not the headline index, however. Social Security uses CPI-W, CNBC reports, and that index is the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, built around one group's spending. A news story about "CPI" and the figure behind a benefit check can therefore describe the same month with two different readings.

The two readings do part ways. Over the 12 months to February 2026, headline CPI rose 2.4% and CPI-W rose 2.2%, according to , so the number in the news overstated the one that matters for checks. Retirees received a 2.8% raise in 2026, more than either of those readings, because the Social Security Administration typically announces each year's adjustment in October, months before those readings came out. For a retiree, each raise reflects inflation already past rather than prices now.

The two gauges divide household spending in different proportions, so the same price changes can move them by different amounts. The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland explains, in an analysis published in 2014, that the CPI puts a larger share of its basket on housing, while the PCE puts a larger share on medical care. The CPI's tilt toward housing is large: shelter had a weight of 35.238% in the index as of September 2026, according to BLS. Medical care services make up only 6.813% of the CPI. A jump in rents lands harder on the CPI, and a jump in doctor and hospital bills lands harder on the PCE.

Most of the CPI's housing weight is not rent checks or mortgage payments. Its largest piece is owners' equivalent rent, an estimate of what owned homes would rent for, and it makes up 25.853% of the index on its own, according to BLS. When the CPI's housing reading rises, much of that increase is in the estimated rental value of owned homes. Homeowners' actual monthly payments may not have changed at all.

BEA is open about where its own gauge is weakest. "Detailed level estimates are more likely to be either based on judgmental trends or on less reliable source data than estimates at higher level aggregates," BEA said in a note on its consumer spending tables. That warning comes from the agency that makes PCE, and it tells readers how to use the gauge. The headline PCE figure is the firmer number, and a single PCE category deserves more caution than its precise decimal suggests.

Knowing who publishes a gauge tells a reader whose methods shaped the number and where its own maker says it is weak.

The same lag ties each raise to prices from months earlier. The February figures came before the oil shocks tied to the Iran war, CNBC reports, so the cool benefit-index reading may have come just before a jump. Because benefits follow CPI-W, a rise in consumer prices tied to oil feeds into the next raise. "Geo/political tensions are driving up the price of oil right now which will continue to drive up my estimates of the COLA," Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security and Medicare analyst, told CNBC.

Retirees who want to know where their checks are heading should watch CPI-W, not headline CPI or the Fed's PCE.

The two gauges start from different answers to whose bills count. CPI counts only what urban households pay out of their own pockets, leaving out rural areas and any spending that someone else covers for them, according to a 2014 analysis by the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. PCE reaches further and counts costs that others pay on a household's behalf, such as a worker's health insurance when the employer covers it. A premium an employer covers can show up in the Fed's preferred gauge and never appear in CPI, so the two aren't pricing the same set of bills to begin with. The harder gap to spot lies inside categories that carry the same name in both.

A shared label can hide different contents. The Federal Reserve Board reports that PCE takes its software and accessories price straight from a Bureau of Labor Statistics category in the CPI. The CPI item behind it is named Computer Software and Blank Media, yet blank media has a weight of 0% in PCE's software category. The price PCE borrows describes a different basket from the one PCE is meant to measure. In this way, a CPI quirk can enter the Fed's preferred gauge without anyone changing a definition.

The mismatch showed up in the goods inflation that policymakers watch. Over four months, at an annualized pace, core goods prices in the PCE climbed 5.5%, but the pace falls to 2.7% once software is removed, according to the Federal Reserve Board. Software accounted for much of the recent heat in goods prices. Alessandro Barbarino, Anthony Diercks and Stephen Miran, staff at the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, say measurement error may explain part of the category's recent rise. Under a scenario the three built themselves, rather than an official revision, fixing the label mismatch would lower how much software adds to core goods PCE by as much as 25%. That would trim the reading, but it leaves open how much of the rise reflects real price changes.

When PCE goods inflation suddenly runs hot, it is worth asking what sits inside the categories borrowed from CPI before treating the spike as real.

Housing costs are still rising. On a seasonally adjusted basis, shelter rose 0.3% from September to October 2026, according to BLS. Because housing has a heavier weight in the CPI, that increase adds more to the CPI reading than to the PCE reading. Neither set of weights is wrong. Each reflects a different picture of where household money goes, so every headline figure depends partly on how much weight each cost was given.

Before trusting either figure, check whether housing or medical care accounts for most of the change.

Shoppers rarely keep buying the same thing after its price jumps. They switch to something cheaper, and the agencies behind each gauge have to decide how quickly to count that switch. PCE is reweighted more often as shoppers trade down, which tends to leave CPI slightly higher, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. The gap comes from timing. CPI's weights are updated less often than PCE's, and between updates the index keeps counting the pricier item that shoppers have already left behind. In practice, CPI measures what a household used to buy, while PCE measures something closer to what it buys after adapting. A family that has already switched to a cheaper brand can look more squeezed in CPI than it is at the checkout.

Across many months, the slower updates usually put CPI a little above PCE. A reader who follows both numbers would therefore expect CPI to be the hotter one. That edge is a tendency rather than a guarantee, and any single reading can break it. The effect of shoppers trading down is also small. In a given period, other differences between the two gauges can outweigh it and push PCE above CPI.

Don't assume which gauge is higher. The usual order is only a starting point, so check both before deciding whether inflation is cooling or heating up.

#5364. Housing data shocks to the upside: Will we get sub-7% rates for Christmas?

The 10-year yield fell to about 4.82%, improving the setup for sub-7% mortgage rates if spreads tighten. Housing demand indicators stabilized, with weekly pending sales up and purchase applications showing a firmer trend despite tough year-over-year comparisons.   AI Summary

Thanksgiving week has been crazy so far, with a stock rally, stocks selling off, the 10-year yield dropping below 4.85%, tariffs being announced, inflation running hot, low jobless claims, strong GDP data and then — the housing data surprised to the upside! Let’s look at what’s happening as mortgage rates have fallen a tad from recent highs.

As we’ve discussed in the Housing Market Tracker articles over the past few weeks, our weekly pending sales data has stabilized and last week it grew a bit. The housing market took a shock when rates rose aggressively from under 7% in September to 7.61% in early October; that shock really impacted demand, but rates haven’t gone higher than that and have eased a bit since.

Those lower rates stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, which grew last week.

Purchase application data, on the other hand, has moved more noticeably. This index can be very tricky at times because it’s a survey, but to see this growth without rates below 7% is a good sign of stabilization.

Of course, the year-over-year purchase application data is still down big, but last year mortgage rates were roughly 1% lower at this time and we were heading toward a nine-month high in sales last December.

New home sales today beat estimates so much that my first inclination was not to believe it! I expect this number will be revised lower, but it’s still a positive trend. New home sales are basically doing the same thing they have done for 10 years, outside the COVID sales burst. They don’t really go below 570,000, nor do they really break away from 730,000. We are stuck in this range, as the builders are still working in a sub-6 % mortgage market, and thus new home sales are still at 2019 levels. If existing home sales were operating at those levels it would amount to 1-1.3 million more existing home sales. However, the existing home market hasn’t had the luxury of sub-6 % mortgage rates.

One positive note that isn’t getting a lot of play is that the builders are slowly moving their completed units of sale lower. If we want housing starts to ever grow again, this needs to happen and fortunately this number has been falling all year long.

As I am writing this article, the 10-year yield is at 4.82%.

If we want sub-7 % rates for Thanksgiving, Christmas, or New Year’s — as I have written about for weeks — we need the 10-year yield at 4.85% and under. Now, if spreads just improve a little, then we get our sub-7 % mortgage rates for the holidays. It’s been a wild week, folks; enjoy the holiday!

#5363. Microsoft ‘To Do’ users make a big to-do over popular task app’s pending retirement

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:07 pm

Microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal users that Microsoft To Do would be their new home. Now they’re being asked to pack up again.

Microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the company’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”

That’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft says Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Why Microsoft is doing it: The company said putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A new Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”

Users weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday users, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft announced Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

Rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and said it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

Reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent company, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist users may end up back with the people who built it.

#5362. Minelab Invests in the Future of Metal Detecting With Original YouTube Competition Series: Race to the Realm Finals

15 contestants emerge from The Realm app to compete for $100,000 in a four-episode adventure series premiering Dec. 2, with Bass Pro Shops as official basecamp sponsor

CHICAGO, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Minelab, the global leader in metal detecting technology, launches Race to the Realm Finals, an original YouTube competition series that showcases the skill, discovery, and adventure of metal detecting. The four-episode series premieres Wednesday, Dec. 2 on Minelab's YouTube channel with new episodes released every Wednesday through Dec. 23.

Race to the Realm Finals premieres Dec. 2 on Minelab's official YouTube channel @MinelabDetecting

The competition began in The Realm, Minelab's digital community mobile app, where metal detecting enthusiasts competed for a chance to become one of 15 finalists. Now, those contestants will face a series of challenges designed to test their technical skills, instincts, endurance, and ability to perform under pressure. At stake: a $100,000 grand prize and the title of Race to the Realm champion.

The series marks a new chapter in Minelab's investment in the metal detecting community, bringing the passion and expertise of everyday enthusiasts to the screen while introducing new audiences to the hobby.

"Metal detecting has always been driven by curiosity, skill, and the thrill of what you might discover next," said Ben Harvey, president and executive general manager of Minelab. "Race to the Realm is an investment in the people who make this community extraordinary and in the future of the hobby itself. We're creating new ways for enthusiasts to connect, challenge themselves, and share their passion, while showing a much broader audience how much adventure and skill metal detecting has to offer."

From Digital Community to Real-World Competition

Race to the Realm connects Minelab's digital community with a high-stakes, real-world adventure. Through The Realm app, participants engaged in a three-round national competition, earning points through digital challenges, community engagement, and real-world activities. Five competitors from each round advanced, securing their spots among the 15 final contestants.

The original YouTube series takes that competition further with skills and adventure in the spotlight. Across four episodes, contestants must adapt to unfamiliar challenges, make strategic decisions, and put their detecting expertise to work as the stakes rise.

The series also gives viewers a closer look at metal detecting as an evolving, skill-based outdoor pursuit, combining technology, problem-solving, exploration, and the possibility of unexpected discovery.

Bass Pro Shops Joins as Official Basecamp Sponsor

Bass Pro Shops, a leading national outdoor retailer, served as the official basecamp sponsor of Race to the Realm Finals, supporting the competition and connecting the series to the broader outdoor adventure community.

The partnership connects the series to the broader outdoor recreation community and reinforces Minelab's commitment to expanding the reach of metal detecting.

A New Chapter for the Metal Detecting Community

Race to the Realm is part of Minelab's broader effort to build a more connected community and create new opportunities for enthusiasts to share their passion.

Through The Realm app, users can connect with fellow detectorists, share finds and engage with the community. The app will also feature all four episodes of Race to the Realm Finals, along with exclusive finalist interviews and behind-the-scenes content that takes viewers deeper into the competition.

Together, the series and The Realm create new ways for longtime enthusiasts and newcomers to experience metal detecting.

Race to the Realm Finals premieres Dec. 2 on Minelab's official YouTube channel, with new episodes every Wednesday through Dec. 23.

Meet the 15 contestants, follow the competition, and watch the adventure unfold at the Race to the Realm Hub starting Dec. 2.

#5361. Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Fully Connected event

AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.

As inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs. The emergence of continuously learning agents and physical AI applications is further complicating that equation. For CoreWeave Inc., the changing workload mix is altering the economics of infrastructure delivery, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier.

“What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante said. “They’ve got networking; they’ve got storage. They’ve got this software layer, which is observability. They’ve got security in there. They’ve got this closed-loop system between evaluation, observation [and] runtime curating … that’s sort of how they’re saying their software layer is now intact.”

During the Fully Connected event, Vellante and Furrier spoke with CoreWeave executives, technology partners and customers about the technical and economic realities of running artificial intelligence at production scale. (* Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video analysis with Dave Vellante and John Furrier:

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s exclusive coverage of this event:

The commercial value of inference depends on both token volume and delivery speed. Nvidia Corp.’s Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator, which works with its Vera Rubin platform, is attracting interest in financial technology and other sectors that require real-time processing, according to Ian Buck, vice president and general manager of hyperscale and HPC at Nvidia.

“Data centers have a natural cap, and that cap is actually their power,” he told theCUBE. “With every generation of GPU, we make sure that our tokens per watt is upwards of 10 times more efficient. In fact, we saw that with Blackwell — we got, in the end, a 30x improvement in tokens per watt.”

Memory management adds another dimension to AI infrastructure economics as agents engage in increasingly lengthy interactions. A single session involving 500,000 tokens can consume between 5% and 10% of a graphics processing unit’s memory. Retaining session context in persistent storage can reduce costly recalculations, according to Alon Horev, co-founder and chief technology officer of Vast Data Inc.

“You can move a session from one busy GPU to one less busy GPU and move KV cache either over the network or read it from Vast,” he told theCUBE. “Once you look at inference as a distributed problem where you have the opportunity to use GPU memory, CPU memory and Vast across a fleet of machines, you have more optionality and you have more optimized scheduling.”

For AI-native startups, specialized cloud providers offer an alternative to owning capital-intensive infrastructure. LlamaIndex Inc. processes millions of document pages daily for customers in finance, legal services and insurance. Inference accounts for about 75% of its workloads, with training accounting for the remainder, according to Jerry Liu, co-founder and chief executive officer of LlamaIndex.

“We serve a lot of different customers at extremely persistent and also spiky workloads,” he told theCUBE. “We really, really need to make sure that we have the right capacity to serve our customers without getting throttled.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Ian Buck:

Protecting AI infrastructure investments starts on the factory floor. Dell Technologies Inc. has developed modular rack designs to accommodate different power and cooling configurations. Its collaboration with CoreWeave includes integrating the cloud provider’s Racky management software into factory testing and improving liquid-cooling leak detection, according to Sarat Krishnan, director of PowerEdge AI architecture and systems development engineering at Dell.

“It becomes increasingly expensive to remediate and fix something as you go later on in the manufacturing process; [it] becomes extremely expensive if you have to replace something in the data center,” he told theCUBE. “What we have done over the last two years is shift our most complex diagnostics — the ones that are going to capture true hardware failures — further and further left.”

At Cognition AI Inc., continuous model improvement involves training across data centers in multiple countries. The company’s Devin software engineering agent now handles tasks ranging from code development to resolving production issues, according to Chen Goldberg (pictured, left), executive vice president of product and engineering at CoreWeave, and Silas Alberti (right), head of research and founding team at Cognition. To support these learning systems, CoreWeave introduced Forge, a platform that connects inference, evaluation and model refinement and incorporates Agent Lens to trace agent activity.

“If you run a big training run, you’re not just looking at the GPUs, but you also want uptime,” Alberti said during the event. “If just one replica goes down, the whole training run goes down. I think a very important metric is getting to this 99.99% reliability.”

For International Business Machines Corp., the power and cooling demands of newer hardware helped drive its decision to work with CoreWeave. The relationship has since expanded to include joint engineering around identity management and workload isolation through CoreWeave Sandboxes. IBM also benchmarks the performance impact of security controls to inform architectural decisions, according to Brian Belgodere, senior technical staff member at IBM.

“This is a supply chain problem, top to bottom,” Belgodere told theCUBE. “It’s not just the hardware: it’s the firmware, kernel levels, code, your data provenance. Then you get into the whole world of agents, your images. It is an absolute provenance problem.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Brian Belgodere:

For organizations deploying physical AI, implementation time is a key consideration in AI infrastructure economics. Aston Martin F1, whose race cars generate a million data points per second each, operates under strict budget constraints and development deadlines. CoreWeave’s forward-deployed engineering approach brings specialized expertise to those operations, according to Richard Ahlfeld, senior vice president of physical AI at CoreWeave, and Eric Ernst, commercial technology ambassador of AMR GP Ltd., trading as Aston Martin F1.

“We really need people that can be outside of the car development phase and come in with the fresh knowledge of what’s happening in this industry that is moving extremely quickly,” Ernst said during the event. “You can build as many processes as you want, call it agile, whatever you want. You cannot stop that process. You got to hit a deadline.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Richard Ahlfeld and Eric Ernst:

Walden Robotics Inc. uses large-scale virtual simulation to prepare robots for physical deployment. Its robots have been working full production shifts alongside humans since May, performing tasks such as machine tending, parts kitting and subassembly, according to Adrien Gaidon, co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics, and John Mancuso, vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc.

“If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon told theCUBE. “We do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.”

Here’s theCUBE’s full video discussion with John Mancuso and Adrien Gaidon:

#5360. Poundland collapsed into administration, putting 12,000 U.K. jobs at risk

Administrators from AlixPartners are seeking buyers for all or part of the discount chain after owner Gordon Brothers' sale process failed

Poundland went into administration on Wednesday, putting about 12,000 jobs at risk, according to Reuters. Administration is a form of creditor protection.

Restructuring firm AlixPartners was appointed administrator after a sales process run by Poundland's U.S. owner, Gordon Brothers, "did not identify a viable solution for the business as a whole," according to Bloomberg. Clare Kennedy, Daniel Imison and Kevin Wall of AlixPartners are the joint administrators, according to Property Week.

Poundland will keep operating while the administrators look for buyers for the company or its assets, either entirely or piecemeal, according to Reuters. Every shop and distribution center is still open for business. The chain operates about 600 locations spanning the U.K. and Ireland, according to Bloomberg.

"Our priority now is to work with all stakeholders, including representatives from government and [trade union] Usdaw, as we identify the best possible route forward," a spokesperson for the administrators said, according to Property Week.

Last year, Gordon Brothers acquired Poundland from Pepco Group for £1 ($1.31), then restructured the chain, closing 149 stores and cutting about 2,200 jobs, according to Bloomberg. Gordon Brothers said it injected £85 million ($111 million) of fresh funding after every other potential backer declined to step in, according to Property Week. It also said the business could still be hurt by inflation or a slide in sales.

U.K. lawmakers allege that Gordon Brothers pulled millions of pounds out of the retailer and left it short of the money to pay suppliers ahead of Christmas, according to Bloomberg. Gordon Brothers rejected the accusation, saying it has made funding available to the business.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham had called on Gordon Brothers to prevent the collapse, according to Bloomberg. "The news that it has gone into administration just weeks before Christmas will be deeply concerning for workers and their families," Burnham said in a statement, according to Bloomberg.

Parliament's business select committee has asked Mark Newton-Jones, who leads Gordon Brothers' European business, to give evidence in open session about the collapse, according to Bloomberg. The committee wants assurances that Poundland will not have Gordon Brothers, or anyone connected to it, serving as its administrator, liquidator or in any other insolvency capacity.

Retail trade union Usdaw has asked the administrators for an urgent meeting, according to Bloomberg.

#5359. Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Testing that more closely replicates the company’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company says it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software update that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July update was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report says.

The preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also plans to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft says its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft said the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”

The new testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the company says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

#5357. New home sales surge in October, but demand signals remain soft

New home sales rose 14.2% in October to a 701,000 annual rate and were up 7.5% year over year. Builder confidence in November came in at a nearly 15-year low, raising questions about whether the sales spike will hold. Stay tuned for a revision next month.  AI Summary

New home sales blipped above expectations in October, handing homebuilders a slice of better-than-worse, Thanksgiving-time, good news. However, NAHB’s November homebuilder confidence gauge had plunged to its lowest level in nearly 15 years, signaling that builders remain pessimistic about the market’s current state and foreseeable-future direction.

According to U.S. Census Bureau data, sales of newly constructed single-family homes in October came in at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 701,000, up 14.2% month-over month, and a 7.5% gain from the same month a year prior. Meanwhile, the median sales price of new homes sold in October was $391,000, down 0.3% from September and 3.2% from a year ago.

October’s better-than-forecast results may surprise many, but they come with a catch: the survey’s margin of error and data collection cycle. They could be revised downward next month.

“A downward revision to September helps explain the size of October’s 14.2% rebound, the largest monthly gain since November 2025,” First American Deputy Chief Economist Odeta Kushi said in a statement.

New home for-sale inventory also tightened, coinciding with a decline in new residential construction. The seasonally adjusted estimate of new homes for sale at the end of October was 470,000, down 1.5% from September’s 477,000, and 4.1% below the 490,000 recorded in October 2025. At the current sales rate, that represents a supply of 8.0 months, a 14% improvement from 9.3 months in September and 11.1% from 9.0 months a year earlier.

October’s sales results may be less of a bright spot than they appear, and one strong month doesn’t erase the warning signs flashing across the new home market.

Plenty of indications suggest homebuilders are working through one of the toughest housing markets in years, including homebuilder confidence at its lowest point since the tail end of the Great Financial Crisis.

For example, mortgage applications for new-home purchases fell 13.6% year over year in October, a sign that rising mortgage rates and low consumer confidence continue to weigh on demand. The existing-home market is also struggling, with the National Association of Realtors reporting that pending home sales fell to another record low in October.

NAHB also reports that, in November, homebuilders had a bleak view of current sales conditions, future sales expectations for the next six months and prospective buyer traffic.

“Persistent housing affordability challenges, including elevated home prices and mortgage rates, continue to weigh on prospective buyers and constrain demand,” Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington, NAHB Assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis, wrote in a note following today’s new home sales release. “Builders are using sales incentives and price adjustments to attract buyers, but affordability remains a significant obstacle to a sustained recovery in housing demand.”

A review of the latest earnings calls from 14 publicly traded homebuilders reveals that the country’s largest builders faced a challenging third quarter, with sales conditions remaining weak heading into the final months of the year, consistent with NAHB’s data.

Last quarter, only three of the public homebuilders — Smith Douglas Homes, Toll Brothers and Green Brick Partners — reported year-over-year increases in new orders. However, nearly all 14 experienced sequential declines in orders, many exceeding 20%, pointing to a further deterioration in demand.

Sales volume followed a similar trend. Only Smith Douglas Homes and LGI Homes reported year-over-year increases in homes sold,

Meanwhile, just two builders, Toll Brothers (2.4%) and Hovnanian Enterprises (0.4%), posted year-over-year increases in average sales prices. Toll’s luxury-focused buyer base is generally less sensitive to mortgage rates and economic volatility, while Hovnanian has increasingly shifted its product mix toward move-up and active-adult buyers, who tend to be more resilient to broader market pressures.

Many public homebuilders reported in October and November that buyers remain very cautious, which helped dampen sales volume and prices.

“As we moved through the quarter, our buyers became more cautious, did not feel an urgency to transact and felt more comfortable moving to the sidelines,” Century Communities Executive Chairman Dale Francescon said during an earnings call on October 28.

Paul Romanowski, President and CEO at D.R. Horton, acknowledged that October was another challenging month.

“Demand did get weaker as the quarter went on, for sure. As rates rose and as we got into October, what we’ve seen mirrors September. Traffic and sales activity are somewhat below what we’d anticipate in a typical seasonal pattern,” he said during an earnings call on October 29.

Against this backdrop, it remains unclear whether October’s sales rebound reflects a meaningful improvement in demand or a temporary spike that could show up next month as a downward revision.

“Looking ahead, the question is whether enough buyers will follow those who signed contracts in October,” Kushi said, pointing to falling mortgage applications for new homes and low homebuilder confidence. “Builders are finding ways to make the monthly payment work for some buyers, but softer buyer traffic and fewer mortgage applications point to a tough winter.”

#5355. U.S. new home sales jumped to a 10-month high in October, beating forecasts

Sales rose 14.2% to a 701,000 annual rate while the median price fell 3.2% from a year earlier and supply shrank to 8.0 months

The Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development reported on Wednesday that sales of new single-family houses rose 14.2% in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 701,000. September's rate was 614,000.

Builders offered lower prices to entice shoppers, and October's pace was the strongest since December 2025, according to Reuters.

Economists surveyed by Reuters had expected sales to slow to a pace of 650,000 from September's initially reported 676,000. October sales were 7.5% above the 652,000 rate of October 2025.

The median sales price of new houses sold in October was $391,300, down 0.3% from $392,600 in September and down 3.2% from $404,200 a year earlier, the Census Bureau said. The average sales price was $459,900, down 12.1% from $523,400 in October 2025.

The estimated inventory of new houses for sale at the end of October was 470,000, down 1.5% from September, the Census Bureau said. That equals a supply of 8.0 months at the current sales rate, compared with 9.3 months in September.

A National Association of Home Builders survey found that 46% of builders lowered prices in November, versus roughly 43% in October, according to Reuters. The typical rate for a 30-year fixed home loan stood at 7.28% last week.

By region, sales in the South climbed by upwards of 36%, reaching a peak not seen in over five years, according to Advisor Perspectives. Sales in the Northeast and West slid to their weakest point in over 10 years, while Midwest sales also fell. One in four homes sold in October carried a price tag below $300,000, the largest proportion since 2021.

The Census Bureau said the 14.2% monthly change carries a margin of error of 22.6%.

The National Association of Realtors reported a 5.5% drop in existing-home sales for October on Nov. 12, bringing sales to a 3.75 million annual rate, the lowest level since August 2010. The group said the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September.
